utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is case IT-96-21-A, the Prosecutor versus Delalic and others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, first of all, in relation to the number of people who were freed, if that's the right word, by the Prosecutor's application, there is nothing before us that there are any more than the persons who are nominated in her press release. We have no information before us that there were more than the 14. I've checked right through the submissions. There's nothing in there. And this figure of 16 seems to be something which is either an error or completely unsubstantiated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can explain that. I think the misunderstanding arises from the fact that there were 11 names on the Omarska indictment that were withdrawn and 5 in the Keraterm indictment, so 11 and 5 makes 16. But in fact there were two accused whose names were on both indictments, but they were counted twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: If I could just mention also, because the question, I think, was asked by Your Honour Judge Riad yesterday whether there were any other indictments withdrawn against accused, particularly in relation to after arrest. I am informed that an indictment was withdrawn against one accused in the Kupreskic case -- that was Marinko Katava -- which was after arrest, but the justification for the withdrawal in that case was not the same as that in relation to the other 14 accused. That related to the sufficiency of the evidence. And one other question that I think Your Honour Judge Riad asked was the number of Bosnian Muslims who were being indicted by the Tribunal overall. Again, I've been informed that at this stage the only Bosnian Muslims who have been indicted publicly by this Tribunal are those in the present case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, before we resume, we have become painfully aware of the fact that a number of counsel on both sides of the room have been merely reading out the submissions which they have already made in writing. I think we have tried to make it clear at all times: You must proceed upon the assumption that we have become familiar with those written submissions, and we do not need them being read out again. Now, Ms. Sinatra, we've come to the diminished responsibility ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Your Honours. Well, then I may have to give a very truncated version of what I was going to present in argument this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes. I understand your concerns. I don't know if I do repeat myself. I did want to bring to the Court's attention several matters that caused the confusion in this case, and therefore it would be citing certain paragraphs in the judgement itself. And for the sake of clarity and expediency, I was going to have them placed on the computer monitor as I make my comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, not if it's going to take extra time. We do have access to the written documents and we don't want them read out. Now, that can't be clearer than that, Ms. Sinatra. If I may say so, checking your written submissions yesterday, I do not think you added anything until you were asked some questions. Now, please just take us to what you want to add to those written submissions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I do find that it's unfortunate that on Thursday morning we have come to this procedural change, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's not a procedural change. I'm sorry to interrupt. It was announced at the very beginning that you were not simply to read out your written submissions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I do remember that. Correct. Well, then I have basically three issues to deal with, and I do want to thank Mr. Staker, who provided an article yesterday, which I'm sure he will provide to the Appeals Chamber in a few moments, that is from the most current issue of the American Journal of International Law. And basically when you see this article, you will see it asks the same questions that appellant Landzo was asking of this Court. I think if we looked at it as a flowchart, we have to see that there was fundamental error in the fact that Mr. Landzo was forced to present an affirmative defence, not knowing the parameters of that defence. When a game is played for mortal stakes like this one is, the rules of the game have to be known to both parties before you engage in the game. That way, you have written objective standards that can be applied before the trial begins. That means that the lawyers will know their burden of proof. That means as they prepare that the litigants will know what the offensive issues are and what the defensive issues are, but more importantly, the Judges can take comfort in making rulings that are based upon objective standards. Now, at the Status Conference last month, Judge Hunt asked me a relevant question that will be rampant through our discussions today. I believe, when you are in England or Australia or anywhere that accepts the definition of diminished responsibility based on the Homicide Act of 1957, it results in a conviction of manslaughter if it's proven. Isn't that really still mitigation of punishment? Well, that all depends whether you have a definition to work from. This Tribunal -- and we agree with the Trial Court's definition in wilful killing and murder. Article 2 requires that the mental state, not only the actus rea but the mens rea of the offence be proven, and the mental state is intentional. And Article 3, murder, has also said that the mental state of the accused of intent must be proven by the Prosecution. So when you come to the mental states, this directly is related to the mental state of the accused. There exists in most jurisdictions the premise of insanity, which goes to total acquittal, but -- and I want it clear that Mr. Landzo has never made an assertion of insanity, but if the state of mind is diminished, then the definition for the defence must have some threshold that it has to prove, some threshold it must meet where it would go from acquittal to mitigation of punishment. So that would go from utter calculated specific intent moving through wilful and then on to stark insanity at the other end. The problem is, we had no definition. We didn't know what the threshold was. We didn't know what proof was necessary to reach that threshold. If an accused's mind is considered diminished enough, then there can be no culpable mental state. That means that it would be acquittal. If the diminished responsibility is slight, then it would go to mitigation of punishment. If the culpability is diminished enough then the crime cannot be said to be wilful. Now, if you find that he had a diminished state of mind, you have to decide what that threshold point is. And that's what we never knew during the trial of this case. However, appellant is prepared to accept the explanation of the Trial Chamber in paragraph 1164. In paragraph 1164, the Trial Chamber stated that Sub-rule 67 would indeed appear a complete -- to suggest a complete defence since the words are "without qualification or limitation." In fact, the article that Mr. Staker will be offering to you in a few moments also says that the ICC Statute, Article 31(i) is also without limitation also. Therefore, it suggests a complete defence. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That provision of the ICC Statute has got nothing to do with diminished responsibility, it talks about the destruction, not the reduction.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: It does. The word is used "destroys."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So that it is akin to insanity.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I would also add that if you go further down, "destroys the personal capacity to appreciate the up lawful or capacity to control his or her conduct." You are correct it does seem to lean more towards an insanity defence, and I believe that the word "destroys" substituted for the word "substantial incapacity" makes a big difference, but it does offer a complete defence. And the argument is that since Rule 67 doesn't offer any limitation there, that it could offer a complete defence. I'm not saying that this Court should come up with the decision that it will be a complete defence in the future or not. What our argument is is that a fundamental error was committed because we were forced to present an affirmative defence without the parameters of what that might be. Of course, the only place in our Statute that it's mentioned is Rule 67.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's the other question I have to ask you. You assert in your submissions that the Statute of the ICTY provides that if the special defence is successful, it affects the issue of guilt or innocence. Where in the Statute does it say that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, as an advocate and since there is no definition, I guess we can draw from a conclusion, since there are no limitations on it, that it could be a complete defence or it could be mitigation of punishment, but that begs the issue that there is no definition and it's up to this Court to give us some definition. Even if you give us a definition right now, the fundamental error was created at trial because we were forced to present the defence without any guidance. Unless this Court chooses to believe that some hints given by the arguments in the courtroom were the only thing that Judge Karibi-Whyte discussed was the Homicide Act of 1957, there was no written order, no decision, no rule that we could rely on as we were forced to present our affirmative defence. We have a saying back home that when you are not given the parameters like that, you throw everything against the wall and see what sticks. I hate to say we were forced to throw everything against the wall and see if something stuck at this point, and that's not the way the rights of the accused are supported and justice is seen in a court such as this. Did I answer your question, Judge Hunt?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I understand the argument you're putting. You will, of course, at some stage, come to deal with the issue as to whether this is a defence at all, won't you, rather than matter of mitigation?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the Court treated it as a defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No. We have to deal with this here in this Chamber, and the point has been taken that it is not a defence, it is a matter of mitigation only. Now, that's a matter which, as I pointed out to you at the previous conference, you don't deal with in your written submissions. That's a matter which we would appreciate some assistance from you in this oral hearing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, at this point in the appellate process, I don't believe that the provisions for nullem crimen sine lege our ex post facto application would make a difference as to what definition you come up with right now. Rule 67 provided that it was a defence. The Court required that I filed notice of my affirmative defence. I filed notice in a timely manner. They gave us the order that the burden of proof switches to the defendant at that time. They gave me the standard of proof which was beyond -- I mean, a preponderance of the probabilities or preponderance of the evidence, in our country, and we proceeded on, based on the fact that the Court recognised it as an affirmative defence with the idea that it was an affirmative defence. Now, if this Court decides today that it's not an affirmative defence, that is a retroactive application of what was accepted in the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's not a retroactive change. If the Trial Chamber was wrong in accepting your argument that it was a defence, then it was never a defence. You see, the problem arises as to the powers of the Judges in accepting Rules of Procedure and Evidence to make a provision which provides an affirmative defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And that's been dealt with by this Chamber, that they do not have that power, or they don't have the power to make provisions for an affirmative offence in the Rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, wouldn't the appropriate way to have handled the situation, instead of treating it as an affirmative offence all the way through the trial, listening to months of expert witness testimony on the defence of diminished mental responsibility and the case in chief, not at the sentencing hearing, wouldn't it have been that when I raised the issue in 1997, that a plenary session should have been held and some definition should have been decided at that point, not after the fact?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The plenary has no power to define those things. Now, let's just look at it. If there was never a defence -- after all, the Rule, the same Rule talks about the defence of alibi, and you don't suggest that's a defence, do you?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: It's something that -- no, it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's a very loose use of the term "defence," which all criminal lawyers unfortunately use. It is nevertheless not a defence, is it, the question of alibi?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Alibi was not mentioned in "b."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no. Look, please. The same Rule refers to a defence of alibi, and that's not a defence, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: No. That's an element that the Prosecution has to prove.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: But that is not in "b." "B" suggests -- tells us that we have an affirmative defence to rely upon. "A" talks about alibi, and it's talked about in the context of the notice that is necessary. So when it has "a" as alibi and "b" as affirmative defences, we're allowed to rely on what the Rule says. And we relied upon that, and nobody told us differently during the whole procedure of the trial. Now, if it were something strictly in mitigation of punishment, the Court should have told us before we presented all our evidence in our case in chief. We would have put it on in sentencing. May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. What happened in our courtroom, in our Chamber, was that everyone was confused. And confusion is very evident from the judgement itself. And first of all, in paragraph 1159, the Trial Chamber said that: "The defence of Esad Landzo has criticised the Trial Chamber for failure to lay down the legal test to be applied. The defence submits that it was forced to present its evidence of a special defence without understanding the burden of proof." Well, that's not true. On June 18th, 1998, the Court gave us, in an order, the burden of proof. It also said that the burden switched to the defendant. And in the next paragraph, in 1160, there's further confusion as to why the Trial Chamber didn't even understand what it was we were asking for. In paragraph 1160, what the Trial Chamber has omitted to do, it says, and we believe should not do, is to outline the evidence. We were never asking the Trial Chamber to tell us what evidence we had to prove.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Sinatra, all of this is in your written submission, very clearly and repetitively.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry that the brief was written in a repetitive manner and I'll try to go forward. I will reurge the Appeals Chamber to look at the confusion. I don't believe that this paragraph is in the brief where the Trial Chamber did come to a conclusion. And when the Trial Chamber came to a conclusion that the affirmative defence of diminished mental responsibility had not been met, we have a right to know what criteria, what legal parameters, they used to come up with their findings of fact, their findings of law. Basically, what has happened is we have, and I'm just talking about the error in law, because I don't even think we need to address the errors in fact if this Court would recognise that an error in law was committed. In the judgement, in III(h), which is Construction of Criminal Statutes, we merely accept and urge you to reread and apply paragraphs 402 through 413, which talk about the fundamental principles of certainty and how the Court believes that that is something that should be evident throughout the creation and implementation of this Tribunal. And the principles, of course, that we rely on, and that the Trial Chamber relied on but didn't apply, are the principles of nullem crimen sine lege and ex post facto law and the requirement of specificity and lack of ambiguity in criminal statutes. The refusal to tell appellant the legal parameters of his defence, preferring to construct them after trial, was an abdication of the Trial Chamber's obligation to perform its judicial duties. Now, I know this is -- just in case you find that there was no fundamental error, Judge Hunt has asked: Well, what law is it that you think we should apply, and how is it -- There is an article in this journal that Mr. Staker is going to put before you that asks the same questions. There are many issues that can't make sense. If you accept the Homicide Act of England from 1957, of course we're faced with the conundrum here in this Appellate Chamber. We have no lesser included offences. So what does it mean? I don't know. What I'm asking this Court is to tell us what it means for the future defences that might be raised. I know the Court is well aware of the Homicide Act of 1957, so I'm not going to revisit it, but it does seem the most widely accepted version of the law of diminished mental responsibility. The Prosecution has just handed me some laws from other countries on which they are going to rely. And we have no objections to that. Really and truly, whatever this Court comes up with as far as the affirmative defence of diminished mental responsibility is not something that we're going to argue about. Our argument, and our error, and our violation of Mr. Landzo's rights, lies in the fact that we were not given the definition before we were forced to present the evidence. Now, I'm going to go to the factual errors in the case, and of course we know that the Tadic reasonableness test, that no reasonable trier of fact could have come to this conclusion. And if the Court would just indulge me for 10 minutes, I have a video segment that highlights the conclusions of each expert witness, if you would allow me to play the video segment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The problem with this, Ms. Sinatra, is this: No expert's opinion is relevant unless the factual basis upon which it is based has been established. That's a matter of fundamental law.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And the Trial Chamber held that they were not satisfied by you that that factual basis had been established.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Upon what parameters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: They said that the basis upon which they acted was not accepted. They did not accept your client's evidence. Now, if that's so, there is no question about choosing between experts. The Trial Chamber never said they would accept the Prosecution's expert in preference to your experts; they simply said that your experts' opinions were based upon certain facts and they held that you had not satisfied them that those facts were true.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I do understand your question, Your Honour, and I would like to bring to the Court's attention that that is an erroneous holding by the Trial Chamber, because each one of these expert witnesses said that they didn't rely on the truth of Mr. Landzo's statements, that they were experts trained in the area to spot something called malingering. Malingering is something that these people look for. Malingering is something they can identify whether they're telling the truth or not. That's why the psychological testing was done, because the psychological testing goes over all ethnic boundaries, all possibilities of telling an untruth, and is able to come up with a diagnosis whether the defendant is telling the truth or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: May I suggest that you apply your submissions to that issue, because what the experts may have said is of no relevance unless the factual basis has been established.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, it goes back to the fundamental error in that how could a factual basis be established when we didn't know what it was we had to prove?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We've heard you many times say that. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: So you don't want to see the video segment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I don't see that it's going to assist us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Sinatra, on this particular issue you are telling us that you did not know what was the test applied in terms of what the ICC called motives for which there can be exoneration of mental responsibility. But you well know that before an International Tribunal you have what is called a general principle of law, i.e., principles which are common to a certain number of legal systems, principles which are drawn from the Judges, from the analysis that they make of major legal systems that are in vigour in the world, and it is also the way the redacters of the ICC Statute have gone about drafting the Statute. These general principles of law, surely you must have known about them before making your submissions or presenting your evidence. You are not operating in a legal void. We are not, as an International Tribunal, operating in a legal void. That is the situation we are in.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is absolutely correct. We are not operating in a legal void. And before we started the defence case, I presented the statutes on diminished mental responsibility from many jurisdictions including the former Yugoslavia, Italy, Barbados, from continental-law systems, and from common-law systems, asking the Court to come up with what definition they wanted us to apply, what elements we had to prove, and drawing from the international law, there is nothing settled on that. It does seem -- if I were to answer Judge Hunt's question, it does seem that in most jurisdictions, unless that threshold is met, to be mitigation of punishment. But they didn't give us any guidance. They didn't tell us which law to use at that point. So I had to just throw everything out there and not know where it was going to land or how it was going to be sorted out. Does that answer your question, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you do. Thank you, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, just addressing the issue that Judge Hunt has told me to narrow it down to, the fact that the Trial Chamber said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It was a suggestion, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I appreciate your suggestion, and I will take it, Your Honour. The fact that the Trial Chamber said there was not enough evidence offered to meet whatever threshold that was, they were not satisfied that whatever conclusions the expert witnesses came up with that it would rise to the level of diminished mental responsibility because they did not believe the defendant. I would like for you to revisit the testimony of Dr. Marco Lagazzi from Genoa Italy; from Dr. Alfredo Verde from Italy; from Dr. Miroslav Goreta for Zagreb, Croatia; from Dr. Edward Grippon from the United States; and from Dr. A.M.H. Van Leeuwen, the Dutch expert. Three of these experts were hired by the Court and the Prosecution. They all came to the same conclusion. They all explained how it didn't really -- matter if they knew the truth of what happened in the Celebici prison camp in 1992, then of course they could be more certain about their diagnosis, but the standard that they apply is forensic psychiatric probability. And when you use the test of forensic psychiatric probability, and related the condition that they found existed in Mr. Landzo back to 1992, they all came up with the conclusion, except Mr. Sparr, that he was suffering from diminished mental responsibility at the camp in the summer of 1992, each one of them. Now, I know there's a lot of questions. This article mentioned they all came up with a separate diagnosis; they disagreed. That's not true, and I would like to reurge the Trial Chamber to take a look at Defence Exhibit D82/4. D82/4 is a chart. There are several different international standards for determining diseases of the mind. The American standard is DSM-IV, which almost every one of the psychiatrists from whatever country they came from applied and used and were familiar with. But the more accepted standard now is put out by the World Health Organisation. It's an international standard to be applied, and if this Court does apply some standard in the future, I suggest you use the ICD-X, which is the international standard. These standards are all provided to overlook ethnic differences, cultural differences in the countries, and they -- what happened was different psychiatrists came up with different diagnoses, but if you look at D82/4, they're all on the same axis. They all say the same thing, they just use a slightly different terminology. They're the same personality disorders. Now, I expected that one of the questions the Court would ask is: Why do you think a mental disorder like this, a personality/mental disorder would amount to abnormality of the mind for whatever definition do you do ultimately accept. This is not merely a personality disorder. It was a personality disorder diagnosed by all of the experts, which the Prosecution's expert called a personality trait, overlapped with PTSD, which is an adjustment disorder. Now, all three of the experts said he had PTSD. Dr. Van Leeuwen said it was an adjustment disorder, Dr. Landy Sparr for the Prosecution called it an adjustment disorder. The only difference between PTSD and an adjustment disorder is how long it lasts. They're on the same axis. It's really important for this Court to know that even though the Court didn't accept the psychiatric evidence, they were wrong in not accepting it because they all said the same thing. They just had different linguistic backgrounds to draw from, and when they were saying it, it amounted to an abnormality of the mind as they described it, and the only parameters they had to go by, which each expert witness I used who were forensic psychiatrists. Which means that they would first determine his mental capacity, and then they would relate it to mental responsibility in the area of criminal law, and they came to the conclusion that he had diminished mental responsibility based on the law that I gave them, which was the only one that I had a hint from the Trial Chamber was the Homicide Act of 1957. If I might have a moment. I do believe that the Trial Chamber improperly concluded that they shouldn't accept the evidence of the experts based on Mr. Landzo not telling the truth. If you look back at the record, each one of the experts said that they are trained, able to spot malingering. The psychological testing can go past that. It's never even taken into consideration because the questions and the tests are designed to overlook not telling the truth. And I believe that the appellant did prove it was more likely than not that he was in a diminished state of mental responsibility in 1992. But putting aside the factual errors, as Mr. Ackerman said, the post World War II trials were and are criticised for fashioning the law to fit the facts. Don't allow this Trial Chamber to do that. Do we have any questions, any more questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, not at this stage. Have you concluded on both issues, both grounds of appeal?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes. I addressed the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I do have one question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: The legal test and the factual test.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. In your respond at paragraph 5.32, you take the Prosecution to task for relying upon a -- some testimony that your client enjoyed performing some of the acts with which he is charged and you say that that is false.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I retract that, because I don't know whether it was false or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I was going to ask you, because the doctor said that that is what your client said to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And if I did say that in the response brief, I retract it at this moment. I don't know what he told the psychiatrist; I was not there. If the psychiatrist said he said it, then it must be so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, it was open to the Trial Chamber to accept it, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So that your suggestion that there may have been an intentional violation of the canon of ethics on the part of the Prosecution is withdrawn, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You just read paragraph 5.32 of your reply.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. I don't have it in my possession right at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well then. Well, thank you very much indeed. Mr. Staker. And I repeat what I said earlier about reading out what's already in your written submissions, of which you were also very guilty.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: I take that on board, Your Honour. May it please the Chamber, dealing first with the ground of appeal based on the failure to define the defence of diminished mental responsibility in advance. Our response is simply that it's not the practice of courts to give advisory opinions on the substance of the law before a trial on an issue commences, and Ms. Sinatra has not cited any example of a case where that may have occurred. We don't rule out the possibility that it may be within the discretion of the Trial Chamber to adopt that kind of procedure if it so chose, but that would be a matter within the discretion of the Trial Chamber, and for the Appeals Chamber to intervene on appeal, the standard of review would be an abuse of discretion. Given that it's not the practice of courts to adopt such a procedure, we submit that there would have to be something fairly exceptional that would justify appellate intervention where that procedure is not adopted. We submit that there has been no abuse of discretion shown here. The mere fact that there is uncertainty in the law doesn't render it unjust not to adopt that procedure. It's probably quite normal that trial courts want to wait until the evidence is in so that the legal issues can be analysed in the light of the facts of the case rather than in the abstract, and the Trial Chamber couldn't provide certainty in the law in any event, because whatever it decided may be subject to amendment on appeal after the judgement is given. We also note in our brief our position that the abuse of discretion standard of review requires a showing of prejudice by the appellant, and we submit that no prejudice has been shown here. The appellant has identified no evidence or no legal argument that it failed to put to the Court, to the Trial Chamber, on the ground that it was not foreseeable that that might be relevant. Ms. Sinatra, I think, conceded in her submission that the Defence, in her words, threw everything against the wall. I take that to mean that all the evidence and all the arguments that could have been put were, in fact, put to the Trial Chamber, which would have been taken into account by it in giving its decision. On that basis, we submit that this ground of appeal should be rejected. Unless there are questions, I would proceed to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: The next ground of appeal, which is the rejection of the defence of diminished mental responsibility. As Ms. Sinatra has indicated, in its judgement, the Trial Chamber placed considerable reliance on the English Homicide Act of 1957, and the appellant's brief, no doubt because of this, also places considerable reliance on that statute and on similar statutes in other common-law jurisdictions. As we point out in our response brief, there are obvious difficulties relying on that statute. The main one is that the statute is concerned with circumstances in which a conviction for murder could be reduced to one of manslaughter. Now, there are many crimes within the jurisdiction of this Tribunal that don't involve the killing of the victim, or which don't necessarily involve the killing of a victim, and if that's the case, it's difficult to see what the more general relevance of the Homicide Act is in this Tribunal. The second difficulty is that in this Tribunal, there is no crime of manslaughter to which a conviction for murder might otherwise be reduced, and the appellant's brief, I think, freely admits this and suggests that instead a Trial Chamber might reach a verdict of not guilty by reason of diminished mental capacity. Now, we submit that that is not an application by analogy of the English Homicide Act, it is a result that is entirely different. Our submission is that when trying to define what the position is in relation to mental incapacity, the approach must start from first principles. The first question has to be: What do the Statute and the Rules say? The Statute says nothing. The only Rule that mentions it is Rule 67(A)(ii)(b). That Rule requires the Defence to notify the Prosecution of their intent to offer any defence of diminished or lack of mental responsibility. But that Rule is a procedural provision relating to disclosure. The Rule acknowledges that such defences exist but the Rule doesn't create them and the Rule doesn't define them. In the absence of any provision in the Statute and Rules, resort should then be had to general principles of international law. However, there appears to be a lack of international authorities on the issue also. Even in the case of the two international tribunals, the present case is the only one to have pronounced upon it. The next step would be to seek to identify whether there are any general principles of law recognised by civilised nations within the meaning of Article 38(1)(c) of the Statute of the International Court of Justice. The Prosecution submits that in almost all legal systems there is a recognition of some form of defence or mitigation in cases of mental incapacity. The existence of some such principles, or the need to take account of that, might be regarded as a general principle of law recognised by civilised nations, but the precise content and scope of the rules vary from legal system to legal system so that they can't be defined by reference to general principles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: May I just stop you for a moment there. You said mitigation in cases of mental incapacity. Do you mean limited capacity?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Terminology is perhaps a little bit difficult, given that the labels given to these things vary between different legal systems. Ms. Sinatra has foreshadowed that I will be providing a copy of a journal article to the Bench in due course, and the author of that article in fact uses the term "mental incapacity" as a kind of umbrella term to include lack of mental responsibility and diminished mental responsibility. Whether in the particular legal system it is a complete defence to criminal responsibility or whether it goes to mitigation, it's simply an umbrella term to take account of the fact that the mental illness or other mental incapacities may be taken account of in the criminal justice system in some manner. That, we say, is a general principle of law recognised by civilised nations. The specifics, we say, can't be defined by reference to that. We would say that in the absence of general principles of law recognised by civilised nations that can give us the answer, the Tribunal is left to define these principles itself by reference to the basic aims and objectives of criminal law and international humanitarian law and general principles of justice. In so doing, it can refer by analogy to national legal systems, but in so doing it has to bear in mind the unique character [sic] of international criminal proceedings. It's an expression that was used in the Blaskic subpoena decision at paragraph 23. In our response brief we seek to articulate a definition of these principles which we submit this approach would lead to. And I know that Your Honour has requested me not to repeat material already in our brief, but with your indulgence, because this is the concise statement of what we say the position should be, I would read out paragraph 12.16 of our response brief. We say: "Many provisions of the Statute, and indeed the very name of this Tribunal, contain references to the prosecution of persons 'responsible' for serious violations of international humanitarian law. The plain language of the Statute indicates an intention that accused should be dealt with by the Tribunal according to the degree of their responsibility. "Provided that a person still has at least some mental responsibility for such crimes, there is no obvious reason why they should be excluded from the definition of 'persons responsible for serious violations of international humanitarian law.' The degree of responsibility would, of course, be reflected in any sentence imposed by the Tribunal. However, diminished mental responsibility should afford a complete defence only where it can be concluded that the accused's mental state was such that he or she cannot be held legally responsible for his or her actions at all." And in saying that, I shouldn't talk of diminished mental responsibility being a complete defence; that should be lack of mental responsibility being a complete defence. Our brief then goes on to refer to provisions of national jurisdictions which support this approach. We refer to France, Germany, Italy, South Africa, and the former Yugoslavia. Now, as has been foreshadowed, since our brief was filed, an article on this very issue has appeared in the latest edition of the American Journal of International Law. I provided copies to my colleagues for the Defence and to the Chambers deputy, and I would request that they now be distributed to the Bench, together with copies of three extracts from national legislation which I would ask to be distributed at the same time. The article is by a Peter Krug and it deals with the defence of mental incapacity in the specific context of international prosecutions, and indeed with particular reference to the Trial Chamber's judgement in this case. Its basic thrust, we submit, is the same as that in our response brief, but it provides some additional details and arguments, and in our submission it does much to clarify the issues. I'd refer in particular now to page 328 of that article. And on that page, in the first paragraph, under main heading III, the author observes that in municipal legal systems there are generally three possible consequences that can flow from a finding of "mental incapacity," which is used in inverted commas for the reason that I indicated earlier. First, it can be a complete defence. Secondly, it can be a partial defence in which the defendant will be found guilty of a lesser crime than that with which he or she was charged. The article goes on to label this solution as the English variant, and cites as the main example the English Homicide Act, to which much reference has been made already. The third possibility is that it can provide mitigation of an offender's punishment. And the article goes on to label this solution as the continental variant and cites as examples the law of France, Germany, Italy, Japan, and the Russian Federation. Now, the first of these three possible consequences, the complete defence, is generally applicable where the defendant has a complete lack of mental responsibility. In cases of diminished mental responsibility, usually one of the latter two possibilities will apply. And as the Krug article says on page 329, in the sentence beginning on the third line of the first full paragraph, and I quote: "Perhaps influenced by ongoing medical recognition of nuances in the forms or degrees of mental illness, as well as by the growing belief that criminal sentencing should take into account the individual circumstances of the offender, reduced capacity is a response to the customary, all-or-nothing approach that recognised only two classes of criminal defendants: the sane and the insane." To give examples of the so-called continental variant, I've provided copies of the legislation from three jurisdictions. I'd refer you first to the English translation of Article 12 of the Criminal Code of the SFRY. That's a translation that I found in the Tribunal's library. I can't indicate precisely where it came from. But you'll see that Article 12(1) there provides a complete defence where the defendant, due to mental disease, et cetera, is incapable of understanding the significance of his or her act or unable to control his or her conduct. Article 12(2) then provides for a reduced sentence where the accused's ability to understand the significance of his or her act, or to control his or her conduct, is materially reduced. To give a further example, I would refer then to the French Criminal Code, Article 122-1. I only have this in French, so I will read it out in French and a translation will be provided. The first paragraph of the article reads: [Interpretation] "A person is not criminally responsible if, at the time of the facts, that person was suffering from mental troubles, mental disorder, and neuropsychological disorder, and therefore was not able to really understand and was not able to control his or her acts." The second paragraph then reads: [Interpretation] "The person who, at the time of the facts, was suffering from psychological or neuropsychological disorders that had altered his or her understanding or hampered his or her control over the acts. However, the Tribunal will take this into account when determining the sentence". And just to give one further example, I've provided a copy of an English translation of the German Criminal Code. I have to point out, however, that this English translation is from a book published in 1961. The German Criminal Code seems to have undergone some revision since then. The relevant provision in this translation is Article 51. The present provision is Articles 20 and 21 of the German Criminal Code, but I think the content of it has not changed significantly. Now, the approach in these national legal provisions, in our submission, clearly reflects the distinction made in Rule 67(a)(ii)(b) of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence between the lack of mental responsibility, on the one hand, and diminished mental responsibility on the other. Referring back to the Article that I provided the Court, at pages 330 to 333, the author of the article then goes on to comment on how the two variants, the English variant and the continental variant, can be adapted to international prosecutions. The author points out the difficulty of applying the English variant, and his comments support and add to the submissions in our brief. The English variant may be difficult to apply, as the relevant lesser included offences may be lacking in this Tribunal's jurisdiction. As I've said, there is no crime of manslaughter to which murder can be reduced. The English variant also requires a relevant lesser included offence to be identified for each crime, which may be difficult to do, or at least somewhat artificial. And, for instance, if crimes against humanity and war crimes are equally serious, as the Tadic appeal judgement has now held, it would be impossible, for instance, to reduce a crime against humanity to a war crime in cases of diminished mental responsibility. Furthermore, the whole purpose of the English variant is that the crime for which the conviction is entered will have a lower sentencing range than the crime for which the accused will otherwise have been convicted. Now, this is unnecessary in the Tribunal if we have no mandatory minimum sentences for any crime, and the intended effect is difficult to achieve if all of the crimes in the jurisdiction of the Tribunal have the same maximum penalty of life imprisonment. Now, in contrast to the English variant, the Continental variant is much more flexible. The Trial Chamber's discretion in sentencing enables them to tailor punishments to the crime in general and to take diminished mental responsibility into account as a mitigating factor in sentencing. It enables concerns about fundamental fairness to be addressed without the somewhat artificial constraints imposed by the English variant. And then a further issue, and on this I'd refer to the article once more. It's referred to by the author at pages 332 to 333. Here the author goes on to consider what needs to be proved to establish the existence of diminished mental responsibility if this is going to be taken into account in sentencing. And the author identifies three possibilities. The first possibility is that the accused must show both (1), the existence of a relevant mental condition, meaning a mental disease or an abnormality of mind; and (2), an impaired capacity to control or appreciate one's actions. That's the normal continental variant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Plus also, I should imagine, that it had some effect in relation to the offence which was committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Yes, that would presumably be so, Your Honour. The second possibility identified by the author is a second, less restrictive option, which would require the accused only to show the first requirement, that is, the relevant mental condition, meaning a mental condition in the legal sense, of whatever the legal definition is of medical [sic] condition. And the third option identified by the author is even less restrictive. It permits the Court to use any evidence of the accused's mental condition when imposing sentence, whether or not it would satisfy the medical definition element of a mental incapacity test, and this is obviously the option which is the most favourable to the accused. The author of the article says it's unclear whether it was in fact the second or the third of these possibilities that was applied by the Trial Chamber in this case. But in our submission, it was clearly the third possibility that was applied, which was the possibility that was the most favourable to the accused. And in order to demonstrate this, I'd refer to two paragraphs of the judgement. The first paragraph is paragraph 1186, and I'll read it. It says: "For the reasons stated, the Trial Chamber is not persuaded by the defence of diminished responsibility as canvassed on behalf of Esad Landzo. The Defence does not contend that, at the relevant time, Esad Landzo was unable to distinguish between right and wrong. Although it does appear from the testimony of the experts that Mr. Landzo suffered from a personality disorder, the evidence relating to his inability to control his physical acts on account of abnormality of mind is not at all satisfactory. Indeed, the Trial Chamber is of the view that, despite his personality order [sic], Esad Landzo was quite capable of controlling his actions." So a relevant mental condition was found not to exist. That excludes the first and second of those two possibilities I mentioned. But then the Trial Chamber went on to hold, at paragraph 1283: "While the special defence of diminished responsibility, raised by the Defence, has been rejected by the Trial Chamber above, the Trial Chamber may nonetheless take note of the evidence presented by numerous mental health experts, which collectively reveals a picture of Mr. Landzo's personality traits that contributes to our consideration of appropriate sentence." In other words, while the medical element of diminished medical [sic] responsibility was not established, his mental condition was nonetheless taken into account in sentencing. And while it's impossible to know precisely how much difference this made to the ultimate sentence in this case, a comparison of his sentence to that of his co-accused, Mr. Delic, indicates that the difference may have been significant. Now, the Prosecution does not concede that the Trial Chamber was correct in law in adopting this third approach. In the case of serious violations of international humanitarian law, the Prosecution submits that it would be inappropriate to allow sentences to be reduced significantly merely because the accused was somewhat hot-headed or given to anger or lacking in self-control. It's the first option that is the normal continental variant. The continental variant option is clearly consistent with international standards of justice, and there's no obvious reason why a broader application of the defence of diminished mental responsibility should be justified. However, this is an issue that doesn't necessarily fall for consideration in this appeal. If the Trial Chamber erred in law in this respect, it erred to the significant benefit of the accused. The error cannot justify an appellate remedy in favour of the accused. We, therefore, submit that there was no error of law. Mr. Landzo also claims that the Trial Chamber erred in fact in rejecting his defence of diminished mental responsibility. As I've indicated, under the continental variant, diminished mental responsibility will exist where an accused, by reason of a relevant mental condition, has a reduced ability either (1) to appreciate the wrongfulness of his or her actions; or (2) to control his or her actions. And in respect of these two matters, I refer back to paragraph 1186 of the Trial Chamber's judgement. As to Mr. Landzo's ability to appreciate the wrongfulness of his conduct, the Trial Chamber said in this paragraph that the Defence did not contend that Mr. Landzo was unable to distinguish between right and wrong, and unless the Defence can show from the record that the Defence did, in fact, contend this at trial, this part of the Trial Chamber's finding can hardly be an error of fact. As to Mr. Landzo's ability to control his actions, the Trial Chamber concluded in this paragraph that Mr. Landzo was quite capable of controlling his actions. Was this conclusion so unreasonable that no reasonable trier of fact could have reached it? On this issue, our submissions are set out in some detail in our response brief. I won't repeat them here. As indicated in this brief, the Prosecution expert witness called at trial, expressed the view that diagnosis of personality disorder was not warranted. The views expressed by the Defence expert witnesses were tentative and, we submit, inconclusive. The Defence accepts, as I understand it, that it had the burden of establishing diminished mental responsibility on the balance of probabilities, and in the circumstances, we submit that it was not unreasonable for the Trial Chamber to conclude that the Defence had not discharged that burden. Ms. Sinatra said in her submissions that she accepted that unreasonableness was the relevant standard of review, consistently with the Tadic appeal judgement, but in our submission, what she has effectively asked the Appeals Chamber to do in her submissions is to undertake a de novo review of the evidence and this the Appeals Chamber should not do. Unless I can further assist the Bench, those are my submissions in response to this ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, based on Mr. Staker's reasoning, is he saying that offences need not be defined before we begin trial? Because that's not the same thing as not defining an affirmative defence before we begin trial. He also stated that every civilised system has such a defence. Does the ICTY want to be the only international civilised system without such a defence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Sinatra, I'm wondering, and I would like to ask you if there is no confusion here in your mind between the definition of a crime, and that's something with all the elements that are part of a crime, and if you don't confuse that with the general principles of law that apply to that act, to that crime. I think these are two different things. One the one hand, you have the definition of the crime, and we know it, and that's part of the jurisdiction of our Tribunal. Then you have the general principles of criminal law and the issues of diminished responsibility because of mental disorders, and that's part and parcel of the general principles of criminal law. I think these are two different things.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you're talking about the general principles of law as applied to diminished mental responsibility, that there is a pool out there that we can draw from and that I should have known what the definition was from the general principles of law in the international community. If that's the question, then I would have to respond that there are so many different principles of law, and the definitions of the affirmative defence need to be known before we start trial just as well as the elements of the crime need to be known. No?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not at all. The Prosecutor told earlier on, that in all systems, a Tribunal does not necessarily state the criteria that it's going to apply. They don't necessarily announce that before analysing the case that is in front of itself. A Tribunal is not there to -- it's in an academic institution. A Tribunal is there to make decisions on specific cases and not necessarily announce the principles that it's going to be used. That's been stated earlier on, and I think you should think about it. Now, the principle nullem crimen sine lege, that's a different thing altogether; the no crime if there is no law at the time of a crime. The implementation of the principles of criminal law for these specific crimes and for responsibility, these are all general criminal principles and they are not necessarily defined in advance by the Tribunal before applying them. That's what was told to you while you were on, and I'd like you to think about it, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If I may add to that. This Chamber recently dealt with the very point of nullem crimen and the development of the law in Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, I believe that in all fundamental principles of criminality, though, the accused has the right to know what elements he has to prove before he begins the trial. And I understand what you're saying, that this is not where there was no crime at the time, but when you talk about an affirmative defence, I believe that this deciding it after the fact is an application of ex post facto law. In a civil case where there is no risk of loss of freedom or loss of life, in the United States, of course you can have arguments and then the court can come to findings of fact and conclusions of law. But in a criminal case, the well-established principles of criminality say that the accused has a right to know what it is he has to prove before he is put to the test. And I think that that's the difference that you're talking about, Judge Bennouna, would be maybe a civil case where liberty is not at stake versus a criminal case. But if I might go on. Mr. Staker has referred extensively to this article which I appreciate him giving me at the close of business yesterday. I'm not objecting, because I do believe that this article assists the appellant and the Court, but I do believe that there was a scheduling order as far as new material to be presented would be allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If you have any problem with the time you've had, it would be appropriate for some written submissions to be put in perhaps next week, if you have that real problem. I don't think that articles in journals constitute new material, but, nevertheless, if you seek some extra time, you'd be very welcome to have it, because we would like your assistance in relation to the points that have been raised and based upon the article.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I did have time to review the article last night, and I would just like to distinguish a few points in the article. If the article is to be believed, then on page 318, last sentence, it says that: "It was applied in November of 1998 in the ICTY's Celebici camp judgement in which the Trial Chamber defined diminished responsibility, a concept borrowed from the criminal law of England and Wales." He also comes up with a test that the Celebici Trial Chamber applied, on page 321, last sentence: "In its judgement," and I'm reading from the article, last sentence, "the Trial Chamber established a two-part test for diminished responsibility. At the time of the alleged acts, the accused (1) must have been suffering from an abnormality of mind that; (2) substantially impaired the ability of the accused to control his or her actions." And it also states that: "On the facts the Trial Chamber accepted that Landzo suffered from an abnormality of mind at the time of the acts but rejected this because he failed to satisfy the second part of the test." I don't believe any of this is clear or anything that we could derive from the Trial Chamber judgement. It also states that the five experts had -- there were five experts, one from the Prosecution, three from the Court, and one from the Defence, and that's not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Let's agree that we are going to go to the record of the trial rather than to this article in order to determine what happened there. I think it's been tendered or produced for a different purpose about how the international law might be developed, and that's the only really interesting part of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: That is very interesting, and I did find it illuminating in certain areas that I hadn't even thought about how it would affect the presentation of expert witness testimony, and I think some new rules here at the Tribunal have been passed since I began the trial in 1997. This refers to Rule 76 bis, which talks about expert testimony that didn't exist then. So there have some results of the conclusion from the Celebici Trial Chamber, I believe. I would like to go back to -- Mr. Staker had read from page 329, where he talked about the influence of ongoing medical recognition of nuances in the forms of degrees of mental illness as well as the growing belief that criminal sentencing should take into account the individual circumstances of the offender, reduced capacity as a response to the customary all-or-nothing approach. And he went on to talk about how it really is an all-or-nothing approach, but what the article concludes at the end, on page 335, in the first sentence, is that these excuses are made available because they serve the fundamental fairness and are viewed as an essential component of a culture of legality. And I think that that's something that Mr. Staker also agreed with. Every civilised system has the defence of diminished mental responsibility, and it's outlined before a defendant, an accused is forced to go and defend himself. I have a lot of notes here that really would go back to some kind of moot court competition in law school, and I'm not going to try to challenge everything that Mr. Staker said, but did he read the judgement over and over again, and the last part of the judgement where the Trial Chamber refers to the wrongfulness of his conduct, whether he could tell right from wrong. In any civilised jurisdiction, that goes to insanity, complete lack of mental capacity, and we never asked for that. But to go back to the final -- what it all boils down to is this case cannot be considered fair for Esad Landzo, fair for any accused in this Tribunal who is forced to face up to a conclusion that the Trial Chamber has come to without knowing what it based its decision on. I don't know what test they applied, and we will not know and we cannot know. Therefore, Esad Landzo's conviction and his issues should be remanded for a new trial or this Court should find acquittal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed. We've now got to group 7. Mr. Murphy, you carry the burden of this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Judge Hunt. I have another question for Ms. Sinatra, because I want to be very clear about what she told us. You're telling us that you believe that -- well, you don't really see what sort of test the Chamber has applied, whether it's of the 1957 English Act or another test. You don't see what test was applied. Are you saying there was no criteria applied or do you question, do you challenge the conclusions drawn by the Trial Chamber with regards to the general principle of diminished mental responsibility? I would like to know exactly what you challenge, or maybe you challenge both, because there is still some confusion. You're saying that the Chamber -- are you saying that the Chamber had no test or that it did not apply the right test, and what is, according to you, the right test, or should the Chamber have drawn other conclusions? What conclusions should the Chamber have? I would like to have an answer to this question very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you, because that really sums exactly what I'm saying. I am arguing both, that the Trial Chamber came to the wrong conclusion, but more importantly, whatever conclusion it came to, there is no test that it applied. It applied the wrong test because it didn't have a test to apply at all. If it used insanity, which it alludes to as far as the issue of rightfulness or wrongfulness of his actions or he didn't understand his right or wrong conduct, then that's the wrong test because we never asked for the defence of insanity. But since they never told us and they confused the issue, they could not have possibly come up with the correct conclusion because they didn't apply the correct test or they didn't apply any test at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to you, what is the right test? According to you, what test should be applied?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, I believe that the most prevalent test would be the English Homicide Act of 1957, but seeing the complications that it causes because we have no lesser included offences, unless you want to go back to the Erdemovic decision in the discussion between war crimes and crimes against humanity, we can have any variant of that. I don't really care what the Court comes up with, I just want something to go by, some guidance. And that's what we were asking for in the trial. Just give us the continental system, give us the common-law system, give us a blending, but give us guidance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You yourself do not know what the right test should be.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I really don't know what the right test would be. I submitted that I thought the English Homicide Act, but then we do have so many problems, because it reduces it to manslaughter, which again, to Judge Hunt, as he stated, is still really just an issue in mitigation of punishment. So I'm not saying that it goes completely one way or the other. We just didn't know. And all we're asking for is the Court to tell us what they think is the right test, and that's what we wanted before June of 1998, before we were forced to put on our evidence of the affirmative defence. I don't know if I'm making any sense. I'm trying to explain our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask your indulgence just extraordinarily briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But you are not taking any part in this; in fact, you've made it very clear in a reply which you filed that it should have no bearing upon the decision you got.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have nothing to say about this issue at all. It was my understanding that this morning the Prosecutor was to report back regarding all of these new documents, and I've had a conversation with Mr. Farrell and learned that they have decided not to proceed. Since I will be departing after the next session, I think it would at least be appropriate to somehow make that a matter of record before we close this. But they do not, as I understand it, intend to pursue their request that the Trial Chamber leave the matters open with regard to Mr. Delalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Well, thank you for raising it. I had intended to do it later on. Has anything been filed, Mr. Farrell?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Nothing has been filed at the moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is there going to be something filed?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, there will be nothing filed in relation to that. And as a result of the order of the Appeals Chamber, I understand that the case for the Prosecution, therefore, on this appeal will be closed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. There you have it, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Murphy. We have a few moments. We are running behind, so let's start.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: May it please the Court, counsel, distinguished members of the Prosecutor's office. The Court may perhaps be forgiven for wondering who I am after my long silence in this matter. I feel rather like the poet of whom it was once said that he would be remembered long after Shakespeare and Milton had been forgotten, but not until then. And so in that spirit, I do finally come to you to argue three grounds of appeal, identified as Esad Landzo's second, third, and fourth ground, and of course these appeals, grounds of appeal, have been adopted or joined in at this time by the appellants Delic and Mucic. And I will, of course, come to each of those grounds of appeal specifically, but before I do, it may be convenient to address to the Appeals Chamber certain matters which really apply to all three of them and which can conveniently be dealt with at the same time. In beginning, I need to ask the Appeals Chamber to do one thing. We have now spent three days, a little more than three days, discussing in great detail the substantive merits of the case, the issues of law, to some extent the issues of fact. These grounds of appeal, however, are not concerned with the substantive merits of the case at all. In fact, they address the only thing which could be possibly more important than the substantive merits of the case, which I'm going to characterise as the rule of law. And by that phrase, let me explain that I simply mean this: that in all civilised legal systems, the accused enjoys the right to a fair trial, and in addition to that, a somewhat different matter, the right to a trial which is seen to be fair. When I use the phrase "the rule of law," I simply do not invoke any higher concept than that. It's a matter of practicality, but nonetheless a very important one, and it's important for me to seek to emphasise to the Appeals Chamber at the outset that we now must move our minds away from any opinions we may have formed, or that the Trial Chamber formed, regarding the guilt or innocence of the accused on any one of the charges brought against them. The matters which we now address are simply quite different from that, and one of the most difficult judicial functions, I suspect, is to put aside those considerations for a time to talk about the fairness of the trial and the appearance of fairness of the trial that the accused were entitled to. Now, if I may -- and Your Honour, I take it that Your Honour would wish to take the break almost now, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If this is a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: It would be a convenient moment, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Murphy. We'll resume at 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Murphy. Oh, I'm sorry. Yes, Mr. Morrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to deal with one matter, because it really fits in with the matters raised as to the new documents alluded to by my learned friend Mr. Ackerman. The position is that if the Prosecution are not going to seek to put any more material before the Court for Mucic, we are satisfied with that and we will not be seeking to put any further material before the Court, subject to one caveat. We've seen a number of the documents. We haven't seen all of the documents. If we could have the indulgence of the Court for 24 hours, the chances are very high indeed that we will not be pursuing this matter any further at all. But with an abundance of caution, until we've actually seen all the documents, I can't make a final determination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I see no reason why you shouldn't have that extra time. Obviously do check everything, but at some stage perhaps something in writing will have to be put before us. We won't be sitting here in 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: I accept that, and of course it won't.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I apologise. I know you haven't called on me. The Prosecution did disclose this morning all documents that would be required pursuant to your order under Rule 66 and 68 that have anything to do with Mr. Mucic. I think the request of Mr. Morrison, if I understand it correctly, is they would like the opportunity to see the other documents. The Prosecution just wants to make it clear that the order was complied with and that the evidence relevant to Mr. Mucic under Rule 66 for material to the Defence, and Rule 68, anything that could potentially be exculpatory, has been given and received and signed for those documents this morning. Mr. Morrison and Mr. Kuzmanovic have been kind enough to approach me at the break and indicate that they would like to see the other documents. That's a matter of consideration for the Office of the Prosecution. I don't think it's going to be much of a concern, but we would like to have the opportunity to look at those other documents. And I've discussed with Mr. Kuzmanovic that I'm happy to meet with him at lunch to discuss that issue and to try and resolve this without any more difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: As long as we get some sort of indication within a reasonable period of the end of the hearing, but I'll, at this stage, leave it to the two of you to sort it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to take a moment to ask the Court's indulgence to say this -- this is in deference to some things that I must say subsequently -- that for myself, I have been involved in the practice and teaching of law, both in England and the United States, for over 30 years. And I say this because in the jurisdiction of England, where I first had my legal experience, a certain latitude was granted to counsel of greater seniority to make submissions in a somewhat more direct manner to the Court -- respectful, but direct -- and it is my duty in this case to make a certain number of submissions that will be of an unusually direct nature, probably more so than that I have had occasion to do in my professional experience up until this time. I would like to begin by reading to the Court some words written by His Honour Judge Nieto-Navia in a decision decided after our briefs were filed in this case, in the Appeals Chamber in the case of Barayagwiza, a case from the Rwandan Tribunal, in which the facts were, of course, very different to the case that we have today. But in his separate declaration in that case, His Honour wrote some words that I think are very pertinent to the present case. He dealt at some length with the duty of the Tribunal to uphold the norms of international criminal law and criminal law as applied by the various civilised legal systems of the world. And he added this: "The International Community needs to be sure that justice is being served, but that it is being served through the application of their Rules and Statutes," that is to say the Tribunal's Rules and Statutes, "which are applied in a consistent and unbiased manner." And he concluded, after a citation from another case: "Difficult as this may be for some to understand, these are the principles which govern proceedings before this Tribunal at all times, even if application of these principles on occasion renders results which, for some, are hard to swallow." Now, I cite those words because what I'm going to ask the Court to do is by any standards a very hard thing, which is to set aside the results of an extremely long trial and not on the grounds of substantive merit but because some of the most basic rights of the accused were not afforded to them in their trial. Now, I referred, before the break, to two fundamental rights which, in my submission, an accused is entitled to before any criminal court regardless of the offence charged and regardless of the nature of the court. These apply alike to Prosecutions for shoplifting in the Magistrate's Court as well as to the very grave offences with which this Tribunal is concerned. And as I said before, these rights can be summarised in the general propositions that the accused entitled to a fair trial and to the appearance of a fair trial. Now, when we analyse what that means, it really comes down, I think, to a series of rather specific rules which we can characterise as fundamental rules of fairness or rules of due process of law or by some other language, but what they come down to in the end is a series of rules, quite few in number, which cannot be broken. Certain lines that cannot be crossed in any criminal case. And because these rules are, I think universally recognised, it is very unusual to find any one of them broken. In the present case, we find that three of them were broken. And we have, of course, submitted a great deal of evidence on this, evidence not in the sense of what was presented to the Trial Chamber but evidence presented to the Appeals Chamber in support of these grounds, and my submissions on the individual grounds will really be confined to just summarising what I think the state of the evidence is. But to summarise, the three rules that cannot be broken in this case but which were broken are these: Firstly, a criminal trial must be conducted in front of a duly qualified Tribunal. And by that I mean that a judge must be qualified in terms of the Statute of the Court or the Tribunal in this case as being a person qualified at that time to hold judicial office. Now, not only must the judge be so qualified at the time when the trial starts, and I think the Prosecution agree with this proposition, but the judge must continue to be qualified at all times throughout the trial. In this case, we believe the evidence demonstrates that Judge Odio-Benito, although of course qualified when she was elected in November of 1993 and subsequently, became disqualified because of her election as vice-president of the Republic of Costa Rica as a result of the February 1998 election. And let me say this: that despite the fact that I shall have some very direct things to say both in relation to Judge Odio-Benito and to Judge Karibi-Whyte, I do not at any time intend personal disrespect to those Judges, but the Appeals Chamber will appreciate that it is my duty to show what happened. The second rule that cannot be broken is that the Judges must not have any conflict of interest arising from their own personal commitment to a cause which is relevant to the subject matter of the proceedings. In the present case, it is common ground, and this is an agreed fact between the Prosecution and the Defence, that Judge Odio-Benito was, throughout the trial, a member of the board of trustees of the United Nations Fund for Victims of Torture. And this really is a good illustration of the fact that we make no personal criticism of the Judge. That's obviously a praiseworthy activity, and we assume all that Judges of the Tribunal are opposed to torture.
