The fact of the matter is that the law -- and again, I don't think there's any real disagreement between Prosecution and the appellants on this -- the law is, if a Judge may have some conflict of that kind which has the potential to create an appearance of bias against an accused there must be a disclosure of that fact by the Judge before trial, and except for the full, informed consent of the defendant, the Judge may not play a role judiciously in that trial. The evidence shows this rule also was broken. The third rule of fundamental fairness that was broken in this trial is that the Judges -- and of course this would apply to jurors in a jurisdiction that employs that method of trial -- must be capable of giving their full and alert concentration to the proceedings sufficiently to enable them to follow the evidence and to render informed and competent rulings on questions of law and fact. In the case of the Presiding Judge, also to make rulings on matters of evidence and procedure throughout the trial that are informed and competent based upon the proceedings. Now, on this issue, of course, we have the extracts tapes, and I suspect that nothing that I or, for that matter, Mr. Yapa may say about that will change any impression that the Appeals Chamber may have already made by looking at them, but I will say, and this may be my only submission to this effect, that when one looks at the extracts tapes, there can be no question that this rule was violated in this case. Again, we make no criticism of Judge Karibi-Whyte. We're sure that whatever his condition was, something was going on that prevented the learned judge from playing that part in the trial. And so we are in the position of looking back at what happened to the Trial Chamber, and two questions really come to mind which must be answered. The first is: Why did the trial continue when this situation -- all these three situations were in effect? Secondly: What if anything should be done about it by this Appeals Chamber? Now, on the first of those questions, I suspect that the answer is this: There was a balance of convenience versus a balance of fairness and the appearance of fairness that had to be assessed at different stages of the trial. Nobody wanted to start the case again, and for understandable reasons. And I do not minimise in anything that I say the consideration of convenience that was certainly in play when the trial was allowed to continue. It was a very long trial. It must have cost an enormous amount of money. I have no idea how much. It involved countless hours of work on the part of the Judges, the Prosecutors, Defence counsel, and of course a good deal of dedication and courage on the part of witnesses in coming forward. Not to reopen this again, but I will also add to that in passing, and not in a critical way but as a legitimate consideration, that these were, in fact, the only Bosnian Muslim accused who had been indicted and brought to trial by this Tribunal. And I don't discount that. It's important. After all, the Tribunal was set up by the Security Council not only to Prosecutor offenders but to contribute to the restoration of peace and security in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and even-handedness in that is not something that I criticise but, rather, would commend. It was a legitimate consideration, and all of those things taken together militated very strongly in favour of continuing the trial at certain points when it became clear that it would have been better to discontinue it. I think there were certain moments, defining moments, in the history of the trial where perhaps, with the wisdom of hindsight, one would have said, "We should have cut our losses. We should have stopped here and begun again." Perhaps the first of those moments was sometime in the early summer of 1997, when it became clear that there was a problem with the powers of concentration of the Presiding Judge. I'll come to that, of course, in more detail. Another defining moment was when Judge Odio-Benito announced her intention to seek nomination as the -- for the vice-presidency of Costa Rica, which I'm not sure we have a date for exactly but it must have occurred before February of 1998. And of course, intertwined with that was the fact that the Judge's term of office was going to end in November of 1997, she was not re-elected, and that was, therefore, a live issue from that time. Again, despite the balance of convenience, it is my submission that at least at that point the trial should have been stopped and should have begun again before a differently constituted Tribunal. Now, Your Honours, this is important not just because of the interests of these appellants, and of course my duty is to represent my client, and I believe it would have been in his interest for the trial to have been started again, but I would also say this, and I ask the Court's indulgence because it may be a generality but it may be an important one. The position of international criminal law today is this: We have gone away from the era of the Nuremberg and Tokyo Tribunals, flawed as they might have been, and for the first time we have a Tribunal set up which has the duty to consider war crimes committed not only by the victors in a conflict, but by any person who may have committed them. That is a wonderful step forward. In the future, we may have a permanent international court which will be that duty, but, of course, as Your Honours know, that, at the moment, is somewhat uncertain. At the present time, these tribunals are international criminal law, the future of international criminal law, and what scholars and judges lack look back on what these tribunals did to assess their contribution of the law, my submission is that they will look at one thing in particular. Not the number of convictions obtained -- there will be enough of those -- and not the quality of the jurisprudence, because if I may say so, with respect, that is already well established. What they will do is to look back and say: How seriously did the tribunals take the duty to provide the accused with a fair trial and the appearance of a fair trial? And that can only be really judged when we have a hard case, by which I mean where it costs us something to give the accused that because of the sheer inconvenience in terms of time and expense and all the rest it of it, and this is that case. This is the case which will determine the determination of this Tribunal to uphold the rule of law. And there are many people out there in the former Yugoslavia who are looking to the Tribunal for that, because, Your Honour, when conflict breaks out, the rule of law is amongst the first casualties. Now, if courthouses are destroyed by bombs and mortar, we can rebuild them; and if the judiciary and the lawyers are depleted by conflict, others will arise, but if you destroy the rule of law, it cannot be so easily rebuilt. And that's what I perceive to be the importance of this case. And I apologise for sounding jurisprudential or philosophical about it, but this is the reality that Your Honours face. Now, having said that, let me come to address the detail of what happened. And, Your Honour, I don't know whether it would be preferable for me to deal with all three grounds and then invite reply, or whether Your Honour would wish me to deal with them one at a time and then have the Prosecution respond to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We originally gave you the hour to deal with all three together. That seems to be the most sensible way to proceed, seeing that you have them drawn up in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: If Your Honour pleases. Then in that case, Your Honour, let me begin with Landzo's second ground of appeal. That is the one that asserts that Judge Odio-Benito ceased to be qualified as a Judge by reason of her election to -- as vice-president of Costa Rica. And I will not repeat what I have said in my brief, I'll just try and pull together what I think the evidence shows and what we have established. The essential facts are really undisputed. We know that the Judge was elected in 1993 and was due to leave office in November of 1997; she was not re-elected. And an interesting event occurred at that point, because as we know, the Security Council passed a resolution, number 1126, which it is our submission, and until very recently I think was the Prosecution's submission, had the effect of extending the terms of office of the Judges until the conclusion of the Celebici case. And I will return to that because it may be important in another respect. But the undisputed facts also are that at some time before February 1998, Judge Odio-Benito accepted the invitation of the now President Rodrigues to run for office as the second vice-president of Costa Rica. No doubt there was some campaigning involved. We don't know the detail of that, but be that as it may, in the February 1998 election, she was in fact elected to that position. And on the 8th of May of that year, as required by the constitution of Costa Rica, she took the oath of office and became the second vice-president. Now, at some time before that, we learned that there were some discussions, and Judge Odio-Benito, I think, quite frankly and conscientiously told the Tribunal what she intended to do, and at some point, an agreement was arrived at which was to this effect: that the Judge would undertake not to assume any activities or carry out any activities as vice-president until the Celebici case had concluded, and the Tribunal was evidently satisfied that that would remove any problem that there might be arising from her continuing to sit as a Judge while being vice-president. Now, I accept that that arrangement was entered into on all sides with good faith and with the intention of making the best of a situation which was, to say the least, undesirable. Everyone, I think, must have been aware of the implications arising from the situation in terms of the separation of powers, the fact that Costa Rica is a member of the United Nations, the fact that the Judge would hold the third highest executive office in that state at the same time as sitting in a judicial capacity. Those issues, I think, were too obvious to ignore. And it must have been the impression of those concerned that the agreement that was entered into somehow solved that problem. It is our submission that it did not. And although we have entered some degree of tentative evidence to the effect that the Judge did, in fact, engage in at least some activities as vice-president elect, that really is not the main point. Our main submission is that whatever happened, whatever Judge Odio-Benito did or did not do, this agreement was, from the first, a house of cards. And it was a house of cards because it did not address the fundamental question of separation of powers that was raised by the situation. It was violative of the constitution of Costa Rica, and it was an agreement that for all practical purposes could not be carried out. Now, as Your Honours will recall, this matter was canvassed during the trial, and there were proceedings in front of the Bureau which were addressed really on the basis of judicial independence, and the bureau's ruling really amounts to this: that there was no breach of judicial independence involved in Judge Odio-Benito becoming vice-president in addition to being a judge. Now, with great respect, and it may be simply because the Bureau was really not briefed as to the real issue here, the real issue here was not one of judicial independence, which would have been addressed presumably under Rule 15 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the issue here was one of qualification under Article 13 of the Statute. Now, both in the Court below, in the Bureau, and most of the way through the preparation of this appeal, the Prosecution appeared to have no objection to the construction of the Constitution of Costa Rica that we had advanced. But at some point, I think in their appellate brief, they indicated they did have a problem as to what the Constitution meant, and for that reason we retained an expert on the law of Costa Rica, whose opinion the Court admitted. Subsequently, the Prosecution retained their own expert, Senor Batalla. And having reviewed that, we had no objection, because in our opinion the two experts said the same thing. And to illustrate this, I will make my argument on this point using only the opinion of Senor Batalla, which was admitted by the Prosecution. And although the Court has it, and I won't read extensively from it, I do wish to look at just one or two things and put a reference in the record. His opinion, on the second page, was in response to a question posed to him by the Prosecution, which reads as follows: "Can a person be elected by the legislative assembly as a magistrate of the Supreme Court of Justice if at the time of that election the person is a vice-president of Costa Rica?" This is on page 2 of Senor Batalla's opinion. The answer he gave, without reading it all, was this: "The provisions under Article 161 of the Constitution are clear to state that the position of magistrate is not compatible with any position of any other branch. Therefore, a magistrate cannot be designated for such a position if at that time he is the vice-president of Costa Rica. There are historical reasons that justify this." And then he goes on to cite part of an opinion from the Constitutional Tribunal. On the next page, just before the quotation at the bottom of page 3, Senor Batalla adds to that: "The body of laws of Costa Rica stipulates in general terms the incompatibility of the positions of magistrate and judge," and a footnote adds that judge and magistrate are the only officials that may administer justice. So the incompatibility of those positions with those positions elected by popular vote, such as the position of vice-president. And the justification lies on the demand of the independence of the judge. Now, perhaps one final reference on page 7 in answer to a question: Would the person in certain circumstances -- that I'll come back to -- would the person be both the magistrate of the Supreme Court of Justice and the vice-president? Senor Batalla says: "In no way may a magistrate hold simultaneously the position of magistrate and the vice-presidency of the Republic. This would compromise the independence of functions that must exist at all times, according to the concept that our constitution has assumed about the division of powers. Under this concept, the same person may not hold two different powers at the same time." Your Honours will note that nothing in those statements really creates any distinction between the situation in which the vice-president is, so to speak, actively being vice-president, in the manner one would expect, or, as the Bureau put it, was being a vice-president in name only. Indeed, it's our position that the contention that a vice-president can be such in name only is a clear violation of Article 135 and Article 136 of the Constitution, for this reason: The vice-presidents, under the Constitution, have only one positive function that is laid down. In all other respects, their function seems to be simply what is delegated to them by the president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Could I just interrupt you for a moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The Prosecution has taken a rather peculiar distinction, made a peculiar distinction, between a grievance as to press cuttings and copies of the Constitution, and they seem to require some formal proof that this is indeed the Constitution of Costa Rica. I notice, of course, that they do rely themselves upon precisely the same edition that at least one of the other parties do. Is there really any point about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that does remain our position, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: How can you rely upon it and they can't?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. One of the questions we asked in our expert opinion, for this very reason -- we had a copy of the Constitution of Costa Rica from a publication from the Tribunal's library. It had the text of the Constitution in the original Spanish and it had an English translation. The date on that copy that we had in the library I think was from 1995. Simply looking at it on its face, it's not clear that the text of those provisions was necessarily the text as in force at the relevant periods for this appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think I've seen exactly the same document you're speaking of, and at the end of it, it identifies which amendments have been made, at the very end of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Possibly, Your Honour, but still --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm trying to see what the point of all this is. It seems to me that if you are both using exactly the same edition and there is no suggestion in the document itself that these relevant provisions -- and they're far more than just 161 -- that we can't rely upon it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Our position, Your Honour, was that if some remedy or relief is being sought on the basis of national law, national law becomes a fact that has to be proved. And it was for that purpose that we asked our expert, in the request for an expert opinion, whether the text in that publication accurately reflected the text as in force at the times material for this appeal, and whether the English translation provided was an accurate English translation of those provisions. Our expert opinion indicated that the provisions we identified were, in fact, as in force at the material time, that the English translation was accurate, and on that basis we would say that there is evidence before the Appeals Chamber in relation to those provisions. But we would submit that simply taking a publication and relying on that as the basis for granting some judicial relief or remedy -- in fact, the relief being sought here is the overturning of the convictions at the end of a trial that lasted a year and a half, and my friends made the point about what the consequences of this is in terms of cost and everything else involved, and we would submit that before that kind of remedy is provided, there must be very clear evidence that the basis for this remedy is well founded. If a provision of national law is being relied upon as persuasive authority in support of a legal argument -- you know, if the law was changed last week, it may not affect the persuasiveness. It shows that for a period this was the law in a particular national jurisdiction, it supports the argument being made. But to grant the remedy that's being requested here, we would submit that there must be a clear foundation from which the granting of that remedy can be made. And we would submit that simply to rely on a publication found in a library, without proof that that was the provision in force at the time, that the translation that's being used in the application of the law by the Appeals Chamber is a correct translation, we would submit that that is not an appropriate basis on which to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And you are going to do nothing to cooperate in obtaining some advice from Costa Rica as to the remainder of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we identified what we considered were the relevant provisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, your answer is you are not going to cooperate; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: I suppose -- well, if the Chamber were to request us to provide --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You have such a request. This must be the most technical of points. I can understand the basis upon which you are putting it, but the fact that you asked your expert, who was there ready and willing to do this only in relation to very few of the articles strikes me as being a little absurd. This document has to be read as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but I would also submit that it is difficult and somewhat expensive to ask an expert --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, either you pay for it or the Tribunal pays for it. It comes out of the same pocket, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour. Out of different budget allocations, no doubt, but by the Tribunal, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, may we leave it to the OTP, if necessary, with negotiation with the Defence Counsel Unit as to who pays for it, that we get some assistance on this point? Or do we have to ring up this expert ourselves?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: We will endeavour to provide the assistance, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we'll proceed at the moment that the document that you've both been referring to is accurate, but that is subject, of course, to it being confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would, with the Court's indulgence, like to take that a little further. There was no dispute by the Prosecution as to the meaning or validity of the constitutional provisions until it was suggested in the appellate brief, in a most indirect manner, that it would be inappropriate to prove them as a matter of law because they were national law provisions. In deference to that, our experts, Senor Villalobos -- and by the way, Your Honour, we had already submitted to the Court, in its entirety, both in Spanish and in English, the Constitution of Costa Rica in exactly the same edition that the Prosecution has relied upon, and Senor Villalobos verified that these indeed were the provisions. The Prosecution indicated that they did not require to cross-examine Senor Villalobos, which would have been a course open to them. They then filed an opinion by their own expert, who independently verifies these provisions. And, Your Honour, with great respect to Mr. Staker, for the Prosecution to raise this issue now, in this indirect fashion, is little short of outrageous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry. I don't have actually in this folder -- it's in another folder back in my room -- your expert's opinion. Does he directly deal with that opinion?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. With the provisions of the Constitution, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That they're accurate and that it's an accurate translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. He deals with those provisions, and as does Senor Batalla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no. The whole document. That's what we need.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think he, in terms, says that the whole document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, that's where Mr. Staker takes the point. I can understand the point he's making. My only concern is that it seems to have been left as some sort of a game between the two sides in this as to who is going to spend some money. We want the assistance and we want to reassure that that document and its translation is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will look at Senor Villalobos' opinion again and -- well, let me look at that over the lunch break, Your Honour, and I will return to that again. But my submission is that what we have here is in fact a normal library edition of the Constitution of Costa Rica, both in Spanish and in English, the entirety of which was placed previously before the Court and was not, as far as we knew, the subject of any dispute at all, particularly because the Prosecution's expert used exactly the same edition. But I will leave that, though, Your Honour, and move on to other things. The Prosecution, Your Honour, also put to their expert a proposition that they had advanced in their appellate brief, at that point without authority, that gave the following possibility of construing Article 161 of the Constitution. They said it is possible that what really happened would be that Vice-President Odio-Benito's election was invalid because she ran for office while being a judge, rather than the other way around. Now, on the face of that, Your Honour, since we know that the Judge was elected and is still the Vice-President of Costa Rica, there is obviously no real factual basis for that. And when they put it to their expert, on page 4 of the opinion, in a form of a very long hypothetical question, or series of questions, beginning the word "suppose," and asked the question: Would the magistrate continue to be a magistrate and that the election as Vice-President be a nullity? The answer, although conceding that that was a theoretical possibility, began with these words: "In the practice, and due to several reasons --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Would you slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. The answer given began with the following words: "In the practice, and due to several reasons, these assumptions are impossible to happen." And of course, Your Honour, as a matter of common sense, we know that the issue here is simply one in terms of Article 13. Now, pulling all this together and analysing what this means, Your Honour, Article 13 of the Statute of this Tribunal, in addition to other qualifications, requires that a judge possess the personal qualifications to be a member of the highest court of the state in which he or she is a member. And no doubt at the time of her initial election, Judge Odio-Benito more than met those qualifications. But the fact of the matter is that as from certainly the 8th of May, 1998, at the latest, but I would submit probably as early as the 1st of February, when the election occurred, Judge Odio-Benito ceased to be a person who was qualified to be a member of the Supreme Court of Costa Rica, and that is a simple application of Article 161 of the Constitution of that state, as both experts agree to be its provisions. Now, this is not simply a matter of academic concern. Obviously, none of that made the Judge any less competent as a judge. None of that influenced any opinion that she was likely to come to on the law or the facts. But what it did was to violate the principle of the separation of powers, which of course is really the purpose of Article 13 of the Statute of this Court, and I think of every international court that has analogous provisions. And there are many -- there are dicta -- again, and I return to the separate declaration of Judge Nieto-Navia in the case that I referred to earlier, where His Honour had occasion to comment on that same issue, although in a very different context. And His Honour wrote this: "The principle of the independence of the judiciary is overriding and should at all times take precedence, faced with any conflict, political pressures, or interference." And, Your Honour, we respectfully adopt those words and would apply them to the present case. And again I remind the Court that this is not a question of the merits of the case insofar as were the accused guilty or innocent, but it is a question of the composition of the Court, and in my respectful submission it is a fundamental matter of such importance that the trial must be declared a nullity. Let me, as a hypothetical example, suggest that if -- very different facts -- suppose that a judge were, halfway through a trial, disbarred in his or her own country because of some alleged misconduct and thereby ceased to be entitled to practice law and to be entitled to be appointed to the highest court of that state. Your Honours, I think there could be no doubt that the result of that would be that the trial would be a nullity as from that point. Your Honour, the trial should have stopped, at the very latest, on the 8th of May. And, Your Honour, furthermore, Article 136 of the Constitution requires that the Vice-President take office on that date and hold office for exactly four years. Now, on the issue of the agreement that was made, clearly it shows a consciousness on the part of the Tribunal that there was a real problem here, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murphy, you have read to us Article 13 of the Statute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Oui.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Murphy, you told us actually you read the Article 13 of the Statute, which says that the Judges have to possess high moral standards and have appropriate qualifications in order to be nominated to the highest positions. However, this article has nothing to do with the separation of powers. It simply means that such a person, that is, such a Judge, has to have certain qualities in terms of ethical qualities and integrity, so these have to be persons who have the necessary qualifications in order to be nominated to the highest judiciary positions in their respective countries. So this is a criterion from which both their moral and professional qualities can be assessed. This article also speaks to their appointment to the highest positions in the country, and this is what you're referring to when you say that Madam Odio-Benito -- the fact that Madam Odio-Benito was appointed to the position of Vice-President was in violation of Article 13. However, to me, Article 13 speaks more to the moral and professional qualities which have to be fulfilled by any judge in order to be appointed or elected to this kind of position. So this is my question to you, Mr. Murphy: Could there have been a confusion between the issue of the separation of powers where Madam Odio-Benito had a conflict between being elected to the position of the highest judiciary position in her country and the seat of a sitting Judge in this Tribunal? So was there an incompatibility between these two appointments? And can you please answer this question and clarify the matter for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, I can. Of course, the Article 13 does directly address both the moral and ethical qualifications to be a Judge, and the legal qualifications, in terms of being experienced in the field of criminal law or international law. And if that were the only qualification, then Article 13 could have stopped at that point. There really would be no purpose in introducing an entirely separate provision that requires the ability to be admitted to practice before the highest court. And, Your Honour, with respect, it is my submission that that provision is related to the separation of powers. Not in the same way as a national law system, obviously we are not dealing here with a case in which Madam Odio-Benito was trying at the same time to be both Vice-President and a member of the Supreme Court, that was not what was going on, but in the adaptation of that principle to an International Tribunal. It laid down the rule that there should be a separation between the judiciary of the Tribunal and any other branch of government of any of the Member States. The reasons for that, Your Honour, are, in my submission, very cogent, because the appearance of fairness demands a separation between the independent judiciary of this Tribunal and the possibility of political activity in the affairs of a Member State of the United Nations, and that's the importance of this. Does that answer Your Honour's question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Murphy. May I ask something?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I agree with you that the separation of powers is a general principle of law. I think that we are not disputing that. But I would like to know how do you apply that principle to this Tribunal; not in general, in concrete to this Tribunal. I wonder, how can this Tribunal be affected by the executive power of Costa Rica, in concrete.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, Costa Rica was and of course is a member of the United Nations. I'm told by counsel, Your Honour, I've just been handed a note that at the time, Costa Rica was also a member of the Security Council, which was -- if true, would mean that that state had direct political and administrative control over the affairs of this Tribunal. Now, Your Honour, the appearance of that -- let me not even address the question of fairness per se but the appearance of fairness to any accused resides in the complete independence of the judiciary, and, of course, that is dealt with in a number of ways by, for example, by the rule that no one country may be represented on the Bench by more than one Judge and so on. Your Honour, that is a very important principle. And we don't contend, Your Honour, that there was any activity on the part of the state of Costa Rica which influenced the present case in any way. That's not the argument. The argument is that as a matter of overriding principle and as enshrined in the Statute of this Tribunal itself, it is required that there be separation between the judiciary and the other branches of government in any of the Member States. This is not an allegation that anything actually happened, it's simply an assertion that there must be complete independence of the judiciary, as Your Honour, if I may say so, eloquently wrote in the opinion that I've referred to. And, Your Honour, it is a matter which, in my submission, is so fundamental that really there are no exceptions to it at all. And we're faced with the fact here that Judge Odio-Benito was, in fact, the vice-president. Let me just add this: Your Honours have a couple of newspaper reports. I don't place great weight on those. In fact, Your Honours, I would really say just this: that one understands the position in which the vice-president must have been, and it was almost inevitable that she would have had to -- she would have been called upon by the president to perform some kind of function. It was an impossible position, and she should never have been put in that position. So I don't rely on those reports as being of great weight but if anything, I use them to illustrate my contention that this agreement was completely ineffective to solve the problem that had been presented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: May I interrupt as well, seeing that you've had a number of interruptions. Your point, as I understand it, is that because Judge Odio-Benito became part of the executive power of Costa Rica, she was thereby not qualified for appointment of the highest judicial offices of Costa Rica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: May I suggest to you that may not have been the intention of the Security Council when it brought the Statute in, to act as a disqualification. You see, at the time when Judge Odio-Benito was originally elected as a Judge to this Tribunal in 1993, she was at that very time the Minister for Justice, and this is stated in the United Nations' own documents. At the time the Security Council did its cull, if that's the right word, to reduce the number of candidates, one imagines that one of the things they checked were the qualifications. And as you point out, Costa Rica was then a member of the Security Council anyway. So as part of her curriculum vitae, Judge Odio-Benito showed that she was, at that very time, the Minister for Justice. In fact, according to her next curriculum vitae, she didn't resign from that position until 1994, and yet the Security Council put her forward to the General Assembly as an appropriate candidate for office. That's one thing I want to draw to your attention. Another is this: Many countries have age qualifications to be a Judge of the highest court in the land. My predecessor in this Tribunal, Sir Ninian Stephen, was aged 70 when he was elected as a Judge of this Tribunal. At that time, he was qualified for appointment to at least one court of the highest nature in Australia, and that was the Supreme Court of New South Wales, which has an age limit of 72. By the time he had concluded his appointment of four years, he was 74 years of age. So he was no longer, at that stage, qualified for appointment to the highest judicial offices in Australia, and yet they put him forward as a Judge who was suitable for and qualified as a candidate for election. It seems that this supports what Judge Bennouna is saying, that all they're interested in there is, that the person is somebody who would have been appropriately appointed to as a Judge of the highest courts of that particular country and that nothing further was of any interest to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: To add to the question of Judge Hunt. Perhaps that will help your reflection, because you refer to Article 13. I will go even further and grant you that Article 13 requires that he would be having the qualifications for appointment to the highest judicial office. According to Mr. Batalla's expert opinion, when asked exactly the same question, perhaps you mentioned when asked: "Would the magistrate continue to be a magistrate and that the election as vice-president is a nullity?" And the answer on page 5: "The magistrate would continue to be magistrate and the election as vice-president would be null." Of course, it is the problem in Costa Rica. As far as he was concerned, he continues to be magistrate, and then even according to your interpretation of Article 13, he fulfils the requirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. May I answer Judge Riad's question first, Your Honour, because I think I can do that quite briefly. It's true, Your Honour. That was the part of the opinion that I referred to earlier where Senor Batalla prefaced that remark by saying that in practice, such a thing was impossible to happen. And at a later stage of his opinion, he also says that a magistrate who even offered himself as a candidate for election to the executive branch would be guilty of an offence under the law of Costa Rica, and, Your Honour, for that reason, clearly that would be a situation in terms of domestic law that would be very unlikely to happen. Your Honour, let me give Your Honour a short answer, and perhaps I can resume after lunch with a longer one. The short answer would be that there is a distinction being made between cases in which, for example, the age of the Judge becomes a factor and where the Judge becomes disqualified for reasons rather more substantive than that. Of course, Your Honour, in Sir Ninian Stephen's case, one can only think that the Tribunal was greatly honoured to have that distinguished Judge present, but, Your Honour, in reference to the question of disqualification all in all, the disqualification based on political office comes from a very different premise than from the personal situation of a Judge in terms of age. And, Your Honour, it may be that in regard to Judge Odio-Benito I need to withdraw my concession that she was eligible at the time of appointment, but I would say that probably, Your Honour, the situation was this: I'm sure that she did in due course resign as Minister of Justice, and I have know doubt that had she not done so, some question would have arisen about the propriety of her continuing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But as a Minister for Justice she was not eligible, on your argument, for election as a Judge of the Supreme Court of Costa Rica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, now, we've interrupted you for the last 15 minutes, and it may be that you were going to finish within the hour. How long do you think you'll be? We're starting having to look at what's going to happen in the future, you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the other two grounds I don't think I'll be very long at all. Probably about 20 minutes, I would think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's all right. It may be that we might have to sit on just a little bit later this evening to finish. I'll talk to the people who matter and whose conditions of service are important, rather than ours, but it may be we'll have to sit on a little bit later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will do my best to speed it up, I promise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll adjourn now until 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m. 24 25 1

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We're very grateful to the assistance of those who translate and type. We will be sitting on till 6.00 in the second session this afternoon. Yes, Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will move ahead as quickly, then, as I can. May I just take a moment to try and answer the question that Your Honour posed to me just before lunch. Your Honour, so far as I indicated, so far as Judge Odio-Benito is concerned, being the Minister of Justice, I feel compelled to say that in my submission, it would only have been proper for her to be elected and confirmed as a Judge on her undertaking to resign that office on her appointment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But on your argument, she wasn't eligible in the first place, so they could not even have put her forward for candidature here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, technically that may be true, but I would assume that it would be acceptable if she gave an undertaking to resign at the moment when her judicial term commenced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, that may be so from the point of view of independence, but we're talking about eligibility here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, you may well be right. And I would just make this additional point, Your Honour. My learned friend Mr. Moran drew my attention over lunch to a case that he had cited in his brief, Hatton versus Raines, in which -- and of course, I cite this as a matter of national law which depends on national provisions, but it is to some extent useful because it does show that there may be cases where a judge, for example, reaches a certain age and has to retire at that point, notwithstanding the fact that he may be in the middle of a case or engaged in his judicial duties. And I would draw this distinction, of course as I myself am only too much aware, advancing age is an involuntary thing over which we have no control. And it may be in the case of Sir Ninian Stephen, for example, the Security Council could, without any difficulty, extend his term of office to complete a case in which he might have been involved, as indeed was done with the Judges in the Celebici case as their terms of office ended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You seem to be accepting the Prosecution's argument about the effect of the extension. I don't think you meant to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, I will come to that point, Your Honour. But in the case of Judge Odio-Benito, this was not an involuntary becoming disqualified; it was a voluntary act on the Judge's part. And I would note this, Your Honour, that in addition to becoming a member of the executive branch of government in Costa Rica, she also became a member of the executive branch of government in relation to this Tribunal, because if Costa Rica was indeed a member of the Security Council, and indeed, just by virtue of its status as a member of the United Nations, she was, in fact, in an executive capacity vis-a-vis this very Tribunal. And Your Honour, that's where the true problem arises here, and no action by the Security Council could have really solved that particular problem. And I think the -- I would submit that there are two things really that indicate that the Tribunal itself accepts the appellant's view of the law here. One is that President Cassese, of course, having realised that the terms of office of the Judges were due to expire in November 1997 and that the trial would not be over by then -- as Your Honours know, we've got the documentation in evidence -- wrote to the Secretary-General and said, "Please have the terms of office of the Judges extended." The Secretary-General prepared a report to that effect and it was endorsed by the Security Council in Resolution 1126. On the Prosecution's argument, none of that was necessary, because if the Judges were qualified to sit at the beginning of the trial, they must have continued to be eligible. And of course, now the Prosecution then says, "Well, the effect of all that was not really to extend the terms of office of the Judges anyway, despite the clear wording of the document," which is, in my submission, completely unambiguous. The Prosecution says, "Well, that's really not what the Security Council did. They created this extraordinary state of being Judges, but not Judges of the Tribunal." And in all candour, Your Honours, I would love to adopt that argument, and seriously considered doing so, because if the Court accepted that argument, that frankly is the end of this appeal, because these accused were tried by three persons who were not Judges at all. But since I do not think that the Court will accept it, I continue to maintain that what happened was what was stated on the face of the documents; namely, that at the request of the President and the Secretary-General, the Security Council did indeed extend the terms of office of the Judges until the end of the case. The second thing that happened, which I think shows that the Tribunal knew that there was a problem, was the agreement itself. If they didn't have a problem with Judge Odio-Benito being vice-president, why was it ever necessary to enter into any form of agreement at all? And the short answer is that, both from a constitutional point of view and from the point of view of fairness to the accused, the Tribunal recognised quite rightly that something had to be done. My submission is that what was done was not sufficient to cure the problem. Your Honour, unless there are any questions on this ground, I will now move to the third ground of appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I will say very little about this. I know my friend Mr. Morrison has one or two observations also. This ground of appeal refers to the fact, which is not disputed, that Judge Odio-Benito was a member of the board of trustees of the UN Fund for Victims of Torture throughout the term of the trial, and in our respectful submission, this situation is analogous to the case that we cited in our brief, the Pinochet case, which the Court has a copy of, decided by the House of Lords in England. The facts are almost exactly the same, and there are only two matters that I would like to address very briefly. The first is that the Prosecution, I think, contends that because in that case Amnesty International had intervened in the proceedings, that added an additional force to Lord Hoffman's disqualification. However, when we review the speeches of Their Lordships, we find that while Amnesty International was an intervenor, while an important point in bringing to light Lord Hoffman's disqualification, was not the ratio of the case at all. The ratio of the case was that any time a judge has such a conflict of interest arising from a cause in which the judge is actively involved, he must make a full disclosure and a positive disclosure of that fact, and in the absence of a full and informed consent by the accused, he may not proceed to act as a judge, and that's what the case was about. The facts are strikingly similar. Lord Hoffman was engaged in activities very similar to those of Judge Odio-Benito. He was, effectively, a director of a fund-raising corporation which raised money for Amnesty International. It was never suggested that he played any part in political activity regarding Senator Pinochet, it was not suggested that he had any actual bias to anyone in the case, but the fact of the matter was that from the appearance of fairness, clearly he did have a conflict of interest, which the House of Lords subsequently said in so many words. And the second thing, Your Honour, and I appreciate that of course Judge Odio-Benito's involvement with the fund was available in documents issued by this Tribunal, but by parity of reasoning, Lord Hoffman's directorship of the corporation was a public record in England which anyone was entitled to inspect, and the Senator's advisors could have found out that information if they had chosen or been informed enough to do so. House of Lords said that none of that mattered. The point was that there must be a positive disclosure. Your Honour, no disclosure was made by Judge Odio-Benito in this case. And yet one has to remember that the House of Lords emphasised it is not necessary to show any actual bias. We do not, for a moment, suggest that there is evidence that Judge Odio-Benito displayed actual bias towards Landzo or the other appellants. The fact of the matter is if there is a reasonable apprehension of bias. Now, Landzo was charged with offences that clearly involved torture, and from point of view, there was a reasonable apprehension of bias, and the law, as stated by Pinochet, is very clear, that the disqualification in these circumstances is automatic. There does not have to be any inquiry further to that fact. I just add this, Your Honour, and very briefly, because I think we refer to it in our brief, but in my submission, when a person accepts the office of a judge, it does place some limitations on otherwise praiseworthy activities that that person may have otherwise engaged in. Judges, with respect, do have an obligation to set themselves apart in some manner from the political fray and the activism on behalf of causes, however praiseworthy those causes may be, because the judicial office requires a degree of impartiality which is not compatible with the kinds of activities in which the Judge and Lord Hoffman were engaged. Your Honour, I know my learned friend Mr. Morrison has other matters on that, so unless there are questions, I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There is one. Article 13 talks about the qualifications of judges in very general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: They should have experience in criminal law, international law, including international humanitarian law and human rights law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And obviously the torture organisation is one which falls within those phrases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It seems to be strange that something should be both a qualification and disqualification at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that's exactly what it is, because certainly the fact that the Judge had that association was a qualification for her judicial office, but what we're saying is that at the time when she became a judge, however, she stepped into a very different role. And certainly with the benefit of that, one could say, Your Honour, equally that a very valuable qualification to be a judge of the Tribunal would be to have prosecutorial experience in another jurisdiction where one had perhaps prosecuted crimes of violence, murder. That would be certainly a very valuable qualification, but of course one couldn't continue with that as well as being a judge. And, Your Honour, the problem arises where a judge is engaged in some form of activism off the bench which has conflict with the kinds of cases being tried. Of course, by definition in this Tribunal, the torture was always a recurring subject. Even if the accused are not directly charged with it, it is often involved in the offences. Landzo was convicted of three counts of torture. And, Your Honour, it seems to me with respect, inescapable that in those circumstances there was a reasonable apprehension of bias which rendered the Judge's participation unfair, and for that reason. Your Honour, her disqualification was absolute, and the trial then must be set aside. I will also say, Your Honour, this is quite consistent also with Rule 15(a) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, which explicitly say that a judge may not sit on a trial or appeal in any case in which the judge has a personal interest or concerning which the judge has or has had any association which might affect his or her impartiality. The Rule goes on to say that it is mandatory for the judge to withdraw in such a case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If that is true, Judge Odio-Benito would have had four years of doing absolutely nothing then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I would regret to say that that may well be the case. And, Your Honour, of course I'm conscious that many -- the Tribunal is in its infancy. Many hard questions are posed by this case, which apparently have not been raised before, but it's the duty of the Court not to shrink from that even though the consequences may indeed be very inconvenient. Unless there are any other question, I'll move to the next ground. Your Honour, the final ground, the infamous fourth ground of appeal, of course, is concerned with Judge Karibi-Whyte. Your Honour, I indicated at the beginning of my submissions that I would have to address the Court in a somewhat direct manner. The Appeals Chamber has seen the extracts tapes that have been prepared, and Your Honours are aware that these extracts tapes are extracts from the videotaped record of the trial, and part of the difficulty, of course, is that the cameras in question, the two cameras which were covering the Presiding Judge, were not trained on him the whole time, and for that reason, we do not have a complete record of the Judge's participation in the trial. The Prosecution has sought to make a statistical argument and say, "Well, of the total number of hours that were viewed, we only see the Judge being potentially asleep for X per cent," I think they came up with something like 6 per cent, "and that's not enough." In our submission, Your Honour, the crucial matter here is: What inference does the Appeals Chamber draw about the periods of time when the cameras were not trained on Judge Karibi-Whyte? Now, I mention at the outset, Your Honours, that probably nothing that I would say on this subject will persuade the Court in any manner different from your own observation of this these extracts tapes, but I will say this quite directly: that certainly in my experience it has been matter of surprise to me, almost of unreality, that I would be standing here arguing this point. I really -- I'm not familiar with the practice in the jurisdictions from which Your Honours come, but I do believe that if I had these facts in front of an Appellate Court in England or the United States, I would find it inconceivable that I would be called upon to argue that what you saw in those extracts tapes could possibly be acceptable. Again, this was not the Judge's fault, but the situation arose where Judge Karibi-Whyte, for whatever reason, and we really don't know why, was at many times soundly asleep, and many other times, although technically perhaps awake, clearly incapable or not following the proceedings. Speaking in a somewhat incoherent manner, and really not being aware sometimes of his surroundings, having to be awoken by Judge Jan, snoring at times. And, Your Honours, my simple submission on this, and I cannot really -- there's nothing else that I can say in argument, but I just make the simple submission that that is completely unacceptable. The Statute of this Tribunal requires that the accused be tried by three judges. The judges, of course, are both judges of the law and of the facts, and in the case of the Presiding Judge, have the additional responsibility of making rulings on evidence and procedure. And when we have a situation like this, first of all, we do not know what view Judge Karibi-Whyte would have taken of the evidence and the law if he had been able to bring his mind fully to bear on it. We do not know what input the Judge would have had in the discussions between the three Judges, what his voice would have been in those discussions, and we cannot speculate about that now. But the fact of the matter was that Landzo and the other appellants were entitled to have the full, alert participation of Judge Karibi-Whyte in these proceedings, and they did not get it. And both from the point of view of having an actual fair trial and, just as importantly, the appearance of a fair trial, leaves this Appeals Chamber, in my submission, no alternative but to order that this trial, this case, be retried before a different panel. Now, the one thing that I do wish to address, of course, Your Honour, is the issue as to whether this ground of appeal was waived. Let me just say this: that it is our submission that -- firstly, I think it's common ground that the Rules of Procedure and Evidence did not prescribe any particular procedure for making an objection of this kind, apart, perhaps, from Rule 15(f), which has since been repealed, according to which the accused would be entitled to make an application to the Presiding Judge to recommend to the president that a particular judge not continue. Now, in the circumstances of this case, the difficulty was that the Presiding Judge was the judge who would be asked to be removed, and so if we were obliged to follow that rule, we would have had the somewhat unedifying position that counsel would have had to address the Judge directly on the issue of his own condition and asked him to write a report to the President concerning himself and a recommendation for his own removal. Your Honour, that, with respect, would not be a realistic position, and certainly from the point of view of an advocate appearing on behalf of an accused, would not be an attractive position in which one should find oneself. Now, the fact of the matter is that the whole rationale behind the idea of waiver, in my submission, is this: That the condition has to be brought to the attention of the Court in such a way that the problem can be remedied while there is still time to remedy it. The simple question is: Was that done? The fact of the matter is that it was done. The Court has the affidavit of Ms. Sinatra, and you know the history of this, but essentially what Ms. Sinatra did was to mention the matter to Mr. Hocking and then to the Registrar in person, Madam de Sampayo, and finally to Judge Cassese. We know, incidentally, that the appellant Landzo, of his own initiative, wrote a letter to Judge Cassese on the same subject, and that as a result of that, there was apparently a hearing -- we don't, of course, know exactly what happened, but there was apparently a hearing during which Judge Karibi-Whyte was invited to present his side of the affair, and that as a result of that, it was apparently ruled that the learned Judge could continue. Based on that, Your Honour, I would submit that it cannot be said that there was a waiver, because both the Trial Chamber, in the person of the Presiding Judge, and the Bureau, was fully informed that there was a problem in the courtroom and they had every opportunity to address it, and that really is the purpose of waiver. Now, Your Honour, it may be that in some national jurisdictions there is a rule requiring one to get up and make an objection on the record at the time, but in my submission, not only did Ms. Sinatra take every step to bring this to the attention of the Tribunal, but I would go further, as I did in our brief, and say that given the obviously delicate nature of this subject, she acted in the very highest traditions of the bar in trying to do this in a way where it could have been taken care of without any embarrassment at all. And if it had been dealt with at that stage, the inevitable result would have been, at a comparatively early stage of the trial, that the trial would have begun again with a different Judge, and a great deal of expense and inconvenience would have been prevented. The fact that that action was not taken is not the fault of these appellants. And, Your Honour, as a final point I would say that while, of course, the Prosecution is entitled to raise the issue of waiver as a matter of law, I would observe that it is, I think, a generally accepted principle in civilised systems of jurisprudence that there is a particular duty on the Prosecution to see that justice is done. The Prosecutors were present in the courtroom throughout what was going on. They took no action of any kind to attempt to assist or to address the problem. And, Your Honour, to the extent there is any fault in this matter at all, it is at least as much at the door of the Prosecution as it is of anybody else. Your Honour, it gives no one, least of all myself, any pleasure to be on my feet arguing a ground of this kind, but the simple fact of the matter is that fairness, and the appearance of fairness, demand that the Appeals Chamber should not uphold convictions in these circumstances. Unless there are any questions, Your Honour, I've concluded my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed, Mr. Murphy. Yes, Mr. Morrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: If it please Your Honour, if I may follow the scheme of Professor Murphy in dealing with all matters at once. A lot of what I might otherwise have said has been said, and I am very conscious of not repeating that which was said in the briefs. One question which may be posed is: Why should an International Tribunal uphold the independence and principles of disqualification of Judges more, perhaps, than a national court, any national court? Well, the answer, it may be simplistic, but it shouldn't be any less; and there is an argument for saying it should be more, and the argument is thus, that this is an ad hoc Tribunal which has been set up to try matters arising out of the conflicts caused by the extremes of national politics. To that extent, questions of politics flow through most of the actions, the hearings, the facts, the determinations of the Tribunal. I do not say, nor do I mean to say, or to suggest in any way, that the Tribunal is political. Quite the opposite. What I'm saying is to prove that it is not political, as it has Judges coming from various backgrounds, advocates coming from various backgrounds, it is even more important that laypeople look to the Tribunal and say, "That is a genuinely independent Tribunal comprised of genuinely independent Judges." There is no basis for any suggestion that there is any form of political influence or political consideration given by any of the Judges to any of the determinations. That sense of confidence, international sense of confidence, can only be enhanced by keeping the rules about judicial independence and disqualification pure and undiluted. None of us, defence lawyers, members of the OTP, or anyone else in this Court, and I, with great respect, include all of the Judges of this Tribunal, should be seeking ingenious ways to circumvent this principle. Rather, we should be seeking plain and simple ways to uphold it. I go to the final paragraph of the Prosecution's reply to the appeal briefs -- their appeal brief of the 2nd of July. It's paragraph 1347, and I read part of it. They start thus: "Bearing in mind the presumption that Judges are capable of discharging their functions impartially, the Prosecution submits that no basis has been established for concluding that there was a reasonable apprehension of bias merely because one of the Judges was to take up a political appointment upon completion of her duties as a Judge." Divide that into two. The first sentence, or the first phrase, "Bearing in mind the presumption that Judges are capable of discharging their functions impartially." Well, where does that presumption come from? Where does the presumption of impartiality come from? It comes from the golden rule of independence. Judges are seen to be impartial because they are independent. So the very matter that the Prosecution raises is, if not the child, certainly the sister of the presumption of independence and fact of independence. Because you may have a presumption of impartiality, but that can only arise out of a fact of independence. You don't presume independence; you see it. You see it in operation as a living thing, through the acts and the determinations of a court. So yes, of course they're right, bearing in mind that the presumption that Judges are capable of discharging their functions impartially is an important foundation judgement of the rule of law and it derives from independence. They go on to say: "The Prosecution submits that no basis has been established, including that there was a reasonable apprehension of bias." It's not the test. Rule 15(A) uses the words, and they're plain words, that there might be -- reasonable apprehension might -- I could use reasonable apprehension just as easily, but let's use the words, the unequivocal words, of Rule 15(A). In response to the arguments of Ms. Sinatra, the Prosecution relied upon, inter alia, I quote, "a plain reading of the Statute." Well, the defence rely upon a plain reading of section 15(A). They go on to say: "Merely because one of the Judges was to take up a political appointment upon completion of her duties as a Judge." Well, the pejorative use of the word "merely" is, in my respectful submission, completely misplaced. This is fundamental; this is not mere. Secondly, that phrase is wrong as a matter of fact and as a matter of law and as a matter of common sense. Her Honour Judge Odio-Benito was not to take up a political appointment on completion of her duties as a Judge; she already had a political appointment. She was Vice-President of Costa Rica. Had she been asked the straightforward question, "Are you the Vice-President of Costa Rica," the only sensible and accurate answer would have been, "Yes. As a matter of fact and as a matter of law, that's what I am." And so the whole basis of the Prosecution's objection is subject to those fundamental misapprehensions and fundamental flaws. My learned friend Professor Murphy has dealt with the question of the possibility of Costa Rica being a party to the proceedings by virtue of being a member of the Security Council. The Prosecution go on to say there is no suggestion, talking of Costa Rica, it had any interest in the outcome of the case, or that it or any member of its government, or indeed any of its citizens, would be affected by the result. Well, of course there isn't, and it doesn't matter. That's not the test. And they go on to say: "No other basis upon which to conclude that the Judge's impartiality might have been affected was suggest in the other party's appeal briefs." Well, that's a matter of determination, and in fact it's wrong. What is instructive to note is that at last we see the word "might" appear, as it appears in Rule 15(A). The issue is not whether there is a presumption of independence. We know there is. The whole point behind judicial independence and disqualification is that nothing should be in place which gives the appearance or apprehension of bias, because that presumption is so vital. If it were otherwise, we wouldn't have Rule 15(A). If Rule 15(A) was meant to say something other than that, which it plainly does, it would say it. These are not rules which have been drafted on the back of a piece of paper by somebody as an afterthought. We all know that the rules that govern this Tribunal were thought about in detail, in conference, by lawyers pouring over papers day after day, in the same way that they're now doing for the Rules of Procedure and Evidence for the proposed International Criminal Court, and it is instructive to note that in the draft papers for the International Criminal Court and almost identical provision to Rule 15(A) is proposed. Why? Because it is so fundamental. My learned friend Mr. Murphy alluded to this suggestion, that as far as the trusteeship of the fund against torture is concerned, the active part of the Pinochet decision was that Amnesty International was an intervener in the action. Again, I repeat what my learned friend said, because it bears repetition: That is only part of the dicta in the case. It is not the ratio in the case. When one reads the ratio in the case, it is plain, it is decisive, it is simple. And although Your Honours have before you the entire transcript of that case, it can't go past a submission of this nature without a very short amount of that being read to you. This is out of the report in 2 Weekly Law Reports 1999. This is a quotation of Lord Widgery, Chief Justice of England, in Regina against Altrincham Justices Ex parte and N. Pennington (1975).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: When you're reading, remember, you do speed up, and you are causing problems for the translators.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: I am sorry. I'll slow down. Normally I only read at the speed which I think, and that's usually pretty slow, so I don't know why I'm going faster. "There is no better known rule of natural justice than the one that a man shall not be judge in his own cause. In its simplest form, this means that a man shall not judge an issue in which he has a direct pecuniary interest. But the rule has been extended far beyond such crude examples and now covers cases in which the judge has such an interest in the parties or the matters in dispute as to make it difficult for him to approach the trial with the impartiality and detachment which the judicial function requires. Accordingly, application may be made to set aside a judgement on the so-called ground of bias without showing any direct pecuniary or propriety interest in the judicial office of concern." A similar view was expressed by Mr. Justice Deane in Webb against The Queen. "The area covered by the doctrine of disqualification by reason of the appearance of bias encompasses at least four distinct, though sometimes overlapping, main categories of the case. The first is disqualification by interest, that is to say, cases where some direct or indirect interest in the proceedings, whether pecuniary or otherwise, gives rise to a reasonable apprehension of prejudice, partiality or prejudgement. "The third category is disqualification by association. It will often overlap the first, and consists of cases where the apprehension of prejudgement, or other bias, results from some direct or indirect relationship, experience, or contact with a person or persons interested in or otherwise involved in the proceedings." It doesn't get, in my respectful submission, much more comprehensive than that. If the Rule is going to be diluted by way of compromise, where does it stop? That's the question which gives rise to the Rule being pure and absolute, because it can't be answered. Once a rule has been compromised, nobody knows where it's going to stop. This is one of those fundamental principles of law, in our submission, that give rise to a very strong and very definite line being drawn in the sand over which no foot should step. And it's no good to say, "Well, I only stepped over it little bit," or "Nobody's going to notice if I step over it at all," because then the rule has been broken; the judicial oath has been, to that degree, invalidated; and it may be strong language, but I think it's proper language because it was the language that concerned the bar of England and Wales during the Pinochet case, and the judiciary, there is a question of honour and duty. We have between us at the bar and the bench an honour and a duty, and the honour and the duty is to be absolutely and completely fair in a pure and undiluted form. Anything less than that is compromise. Anything less than that is seeking an ingenious way around a rule which we all know in our hearts to be the only rule that we can properly work with. Those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Morrison. Now Mr. Yapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: I thank Your Honours. I'm reminded of the direction or the reminder that Your Honour, the Presiding Judge, gave us on the repetition of submissions. I've been trying to keep a check on my checklist and the submissions made by my learned friend Professor Murphy and Mr. Morrison, and I should say that some of the submissions, maybe not all, are submissions that have already been made in the recent submissions, and we have responded to them. There are one or two matters in respect of the three issues that were taken up, three issues that have been taken up by my learned friends, on which I should like to make certain submissions. It was interesting and educative to listen to Mr. Murphy on the subject of the fairness of trial, appearance of fairness. Your Honours, what is important in a criminal trial is to apply those theories to the facts of a case. It was important, it was really necessary for my learned friend to apply what he stated to what really transpired in this case. On the first ground, that Judge Odio-Benito was elected vice-president of Costa Rica and thereby she disqualified herself from being a judge of the Tribunal, there were a number of questions that were asked and not satisfactorily answered. Now, as it was pointed out in her qualifications that were tendered at the time of her appointment, at the time of her election to the prestigious position of a judge of this Tribunal, she was a member of the executive of Costa Rica. She was the Minister of Justice. So that was one of the qualifications that was in the curriculum vitae. It was placed as the qualification of Judge Odio-Benito, and she was appointed to be elected as a judge. Then there is this question that came up about the constitutional provision in Costa Rica which is there at present. At this stage, I should like to refer to a submission made by my colleague Mr. Christopher Staker on the little disagreement that we have with the appellants, or Mr. Murphy, on the proof of the constitution or the provisions before Your Honours. It is -- in respect of the provisions that have been cited by the experts, we have no quarrel. It was stated by Mr. Staker that it may be necessary, for the purpose of formality, that the constitution, when it is introduced, of a national jurisdiction be proved before Your Honours. It is only for that purpose that we stated so. And also, it may be, if we merely agree that it could be placed, it may be a precedent in future cases. It is only for that purpose. But as far as the experts are concerned, in many of the matters we are in agreement. The question that arises is -- now, this submission has been made by Professor Murphy citing the constitutional provision, I think it is Article 161 -- 132 Sub-article 5. Those are the relevant provisions that have been provided. The question arises -- she was a judge of this court, of this Tribunal. Then the question arises: If this argument is to be applied, logically could she have been appointed vice-president in Costa Rica in terms of those provisions? What is important for us here is that she informed the Plenary, she informed the Tribunal that she was going to accept this position whether there was any objection to the acceptance. Then the further undertaking after, when there was no objection, the further undertaking that she gave that she would not be assuming functions as vice-president. That is an important element that has to be taken into account, because we are looking at practical -- a practical situation. It is my submission that in the interpretation of the Rules, in the interpretation of the working of the Tribunal in respect of this matter, that there has to be a pragmatic approach. The learned Judge informed the Tribunal that she would not be assuming functions as vice-president. What does it mean? It goes to the extent of saying that she's nominally a vice-president, she's not functioning as vice-president, but she's continuing as a judge of the Tribunal. That is what matters to the Tribunal. As to whether she could have been appointed vice-president in Costa Rica is another question. If that has to be looked into, then the question arises whether Your Honours are going to interpret the Constitution of Costa Rica, which is not your function. Because anyone could have taken up the objection in Costa Rica -- it is only for purpose of argument I say so -- that she was not qualified or she was not -- she didn't have the qualification to be appointed vice-president. It could have been taken up in Costa Rica, but it is with great respect I submit that Your Honours will not go that far, and it is not necessary for Your Honours to look into that question. What matters is she had the qualifications to be appointed a judge of the Tribunal and she was appointed. Now, there was another question that we have in our submissions that we have taken up in respect of this appointment which had not been responded to or replied to by Professor Murphy but it is in the submissions, and I would like, at this stage, to make a reference to it because it adds on to the pragmatic approach that Your Honours should have. The term of service as a judge of the Tribunal of Judge Odio-Benito was coming to an end, and it became necessary to extend the service, to extend the service for one particular reason; so that the Celebici case could be concluded. I say for one particular reason, because the path that was assigned to that Bench was only that. That was the only task that was assigned to her by the Tribunal or the Security Council. That was the only task; that is, to finish the case, finish the Celebici case. It is for that purpose that the term was extended. Now, there has been reference, Your Honours, to the term "extension." The term "extension" there, in my respectful submission, the term "extension" has to be read with the other wording in the Resolution, that is, to finish the Celebici case. That is only for that purpose. The term "extension" should not be taken out of context and say that it was an extension as a judge of the Tribunal.
