So we say -- as an argument, we say that in that situation, in that special situation of the Judge, that the objection that is taken up in terms of Article 13(i) would not apply. They were not members of the Tribunal. 13(i) applies to members of the Tribunal, and the Resolution says on being replaced, being replaced as members of the Tribunal, it is thereafter only -- if I can get on to the Resolution straight away. If Your Honours will bear with me. These words are important. It says: "Endorses the recommendation of the Secretary-General that Judges Karibi-Whyte, Odio-Benito, and Jan, once replaced as members of this Tribunal, finish this Celebici case that they have begun before the expiry of their terms of office." It is in those terms that the Resolution has been worded, and it was in those terms that the term of service as judges was extended. There is reference to the term of "extension", or the word "extension", in the letter addressed to the General Secretary of the United Nations, the President of the Chamber, and also the Secretary-General's letter to the Security Council and the General Assembly. I made the submission that the term "extension" has to be read in accordance or in conjunction with the words in the Resolution. So it would mean that they were not, so far as the -- so far as the extension was concerned, they were not concerned as members of the Tribunal. So it was a special situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Yapa, I'm sorry, I did not get your last sentence. I did not understand the last sentence. [In English] ... extension was concerned, they were not concerned as members of the Tribunal." [Interpretation] Are they still members of the Tribunal or not any more?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: I beg Your Honour's pardon. I was not able to follow your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you say that, do you mean that the fact that their term of service was extended for the Celebici case? Do you mean to say that they are still members of the Tribunal or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Your Honour, in terms of the Resolution, I can go only up to the wording of the Resolution, the Resolution is: "Once replaced as members of the Tribunal, finish the Celebici case." It says "finish the Celebici case they have begun before expiry of their terms of office." So it may mean -- it may mean that -- there it means, finish the trial of the Celebici case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But as what? I think this is what Judge Bennouna is really after. Are they finishing it as judges of the Tribunal? You say not because they don't have to be qualified to be judges. If you're correct, the Resolution surely would have had to have, at the very least, some deeming provision to make their judgement a judgement of the Tribunal because they are not part of the Tribunal, but it doesn't. Therefore, the judgement they delivered was not a judgement of the Tribunal and it is, therefore, invalid.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: With great respect, my submission was not that they did not continue to be members of the Tribunal , rather, judges of the Tribunal, but their functions were restricted to the Celebici case. That was my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Then they are still judges of the Tribunal but their functions are restricted to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Celebici case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But if they are judges of the Tribunal, they still have to be qualified to be judges, do they not?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, they do. So then what is the point of this further argument of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: It is in respect of the applicability and also the wording of this Resolution that -- because the Resolution says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I don't think you've understood my question. Your argument, as I understand your further argument, the additional argument, is that the requirements of Article 13 no longer apply because, as I had understood you to say, they were no longer judges of the Tribunal. Well, now you do say they are judges of the Tribunal but they had limited functions. If were they judges of the Tribunal, would they not have had to have been qualified to be judges of the Tribunal? And I thought you said then yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, then, what is the point of this additional argument? Because it is exactly the point that the Defence has taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes. But it is -- Your Honour will be pleased to see the qualification we're speaking of is a qualified qualification. It is a qualified qualification. That is my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Yapa, if I may take the liberty of stating what I think is the truth. I think that through this Resolution -- what happened is that, through this Resolution, the Security Council decided that rather than having these judges being elected to sit on the Tribunal as provided for in the Statute, they decided that their term of office would be extended beyond the four years on decision -- after a decision of a Security Council in order to sit on the Celebici trial. It's only the way of appointing them, the mode of appointment that is changed here. They were not elected. It was in a decision of the Security Council. In my opinion, that's the effect of this Resolution, the Resolution you've quoted to us. As for the rest, they have to respect exactly the same requirements, moral requirements, professional requirements, as all the other judges, because they have to try accused defendants and to render a judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: I thank you, Your Honour. I bow to Your Honour's opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Perhaps you better go on with your points, Mr. Yapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: I thank you. Yes. On the next ground that is in respect to membership of the United Nations Voluntary Fund for Victims of Torture, the submission has been right along of Professor Murphy or in the situations made on behalf of Mr. Landzo, is that the case is similar or more or less identical to the Pinochet case that was decided in England. We have taken up the position that it is not identical, that it can be distinguished for very valid reasons. In the Pinochet case, the House of Lords in England looked at the question in two ways. In respect to Lord Hoffman, it was stated -- in analysing the facts of Lord Hoffman's association with Amnesty International, there were two criteria that the House of Lords mentioned. Firstly -- these were two aspects that were considered -- whether -- where a judge is a party, in fact a party to the litigation or has relevant interests in its outcome, in which case the disqualification is automatic. Certainly, they looked into another respect where a judge is not a party to the suit and does not have a relevant interest in the outcome but in some other way the judge's conduct or behaviour may give rise to a suspicion that he or she is not impartial. Now, what is important is when you try to draw a parallel between that case and this case, it was stated in that case that Lord Hoffman, who was the Judge of the House of Lords which decided that case, as stated was disqualified because he was party to the case, because he was a party to the case. Now, they looked into the way in which the particular judge was a party to the case. He was a director of an affiliated association of Amnesty International. Further than that, he had appeared as counsel for Amnesty International on an earlier occasion. Then they looked into the aims and purposes of Amnesty International and held -- one more matter. Amnesty International was permitted to intervene in the case, intervene in the case that was heard before the House of Lords. So there was a situation where the judge presiding had a party before him with whom he had a close association, and he had an interest in what was being pursued by that party. So to that extent they're saying this is an instance where the judge is automatically disqualified. It was a very, very high standard that was adopted by the House of Lords in that case. Now, what is important here is in drawing a parallel, it must be shown, it must be shown by Judge Odio-Benito being a member of the board of trustees of the fund, of the particular fund, if Pinochet is to be brought in, that he was a party, that he had that interest to extent to be disqualified. The mandate has been cited. The mandate of the fund is before Your Honours. If one examines that, what was the purpose of the fund? To provide assistance to victims of torture, victims of torture. That is the only, only relevance of the subject of torture to this case. He was there as a director or a member of the board of trustees. If I may say so, it is a remote connection, a remote connection which should have no influence whatsoever on the outcome of the case, or he would not have any interest on the outcome of the case. What has been attempted to, if this is taken to the logical conclusion, what has been attempted to do is keep judges away from mundane affairs; to keep them cloistered in ivory towers; that they do not have anything to do with interests that -- common interests that people have. They have to keep away to a certain extent, and the extent understood, and it is very clearly explained in Pinochet. Mr. Morrison submitted the standard of reasonable apprehension. Again, it is extremely necessary to use that standard to the facts of this case. On what basis can it be said there was this reasonable apprehension, an apprehension for which you could give a reason? So it is my submission, respectful submission, that it cannot be said by the mere membership of the trust fund, by the mere membership of the board of trustees of the fund, that is referred to the UN fund, that Judge Odio-Benito was disqualified. And one other matter, at the time of her election this was stated. Even at that stage, that was one of her qualifications or how she described herself, that she was a member of the board of trustees, and she was elected. And it goes counter to my learned friend's argument to say that up to the 8th of May, 1998, she was qualified in every way to continue as a judge of the Tribunal. That's something that my learned friend has stated in his written submissions, that she had the qualifications to continue as a judge of the Tribunal. Logically, by reason of argument, then she was not qualified. But she was elected on that qualification, and as whatever qualification that she declared, that she was Minister of Justice, she was elected. So it is my respectful submission that the argument or the submission cannot succeed. I have to make a short submission on the third ground of appeal that has been taken up. I'm not going to make any submissions to Your Honours on the video excerpts that have been provided. They are before Your Honours. They have been examined. But I must mention that on the particulars that were furnished to us, so far as the appellants were concerned, we have examined them and we have provided an analytical survey of all the segments in respect of the time. It may be said statistics will not prove, and it has already been said that we do not know at times when the camera was not on the Judge, not focusing on the Judge, as to whether he slept or not. That is a matter of conjecture what has been produced before Your Honours is to satisfy Your Honours that the Judge slept in certain excerpts from the video recordings that were available. But there is an interesting aspect to this question. The appellant complains that there was prejudice, that there was no fairness, that he did not receive a fair trial. Now, from where does this complaint come? From one source. It comes from one source. There were other accused in the case, there was an array of illustrious counsel defending the accused, but there was no complaint, no complaint whatsoever till the last moment that there was this unfairness, that the case could not be presented. So what is the conclusion that can be arrived at? It is our submission, when the excerpts are examined and our analysis in respect of how it affected this particular accused, that is, Landzo, and how the case has been decided as far as the charges against him were concerned, that there has not been any prejudice, that there has not been any unfairness. It is affirmatively proved from what -- the material that has been presented. Those are my submissions. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, regarding firstly the constitutional ground, the second ground of appeal regarding Judge Odio-Benito's election, the phrase again has been used that Judge Odio-Benito was not only the Vice-President of Costa Rica, but the only positive function that the Constitution of Costa Rica imposes on either one of the Vice-Presidents is to stand available to act in the stead of the president should it be necessary. If during the trial -- and providence be thanked, this did not happen -- some assassin had been successful in killing both the President and the First Vice-President of Costa Rica, Elizabeth Odio-Benito was from that moment, ipso facto, the President of Costa Rica, and there's nothing that could be done about that. That was not something that she -- that was not a function that she could agree not to exercise because it arises by matter of the operation of section 135 of the Constitution. Nothing nominal about that at all. She was, in fact, exercising that function, and the Court may feel that, in a way, that that's the only important function of the Vice-Presidency, because the Constitution really doesn't specify anything else. Yes, she may, at the request of the President, undertake other duties, as indeed we know she did in relation to being a member of the so-called Board of Mediators, but that the Vice-President could choose to do or not to do. But as regards standing in the place of the President, that was a function that devolved upon her from the moment she took the oath, and that was not nominal in any sense of the word. It may be, Your Honour -- I'm not sure -- that where the Prosecution has now abandoned the argument that the Judges were not members of the Tribunal, all I can say about that is, Your Honour, again to say that if that is their submission, and if I have procedural power to do so, I'd move for summary judgement on the hearing of the appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor Murphy, just a little precision that I need on what you have just said and on the fact that Ms. Odio-Benito was Vice-President of Costa Rica. Earlier on in the afternoon you said, speaking about Judge Karibi-Whyte, that in view of Rule 15, there cannot be a waiver, and you said, that is your argument, that there had been no waiver, so we cannot reproach you not to have mentioned that argument. But during trial, was it mentioned that the post of Judge Odio-Benito as Vice-President of Costa Rica had become something which forbade her to sit as a Judge on the trial? Was it said during the trial that it was something that was incompatible with her mandate of Judge of the Tribunal? Or did you say something that was the other way around: The fact that she was a Judge precluded her from being the Vice-President of Costa Rica? Was that question ever put during the trial in order to impeach the Judge during the trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it was. In fact, a motion was made which was considered by the Bureau when it became known that the situation had occurred. And Your Honour, I was not at the trial, so I'm just going on the papers that were filed. But yes, indeed, that point was made. I should say, in fairness to the Bureau, that the main point that was argued in the motion was the one of judicial independence, and it may be that part of the reason why the Bureau may perhaps not have appreciated fully what the situation was was that it was argued more in terms of judicial independence under Rule 15. But if Your Honour looks at the papers in that motion, yes, it was brought to the attention of the Bureau that she was disqualified, and I'm told that that was filed in May of 1998, Your Honour, before the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And did the Bureau come to a decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, they did, and they decided that in light of the Judge's undertakings not to undertake any activities, it would be permissible for her to continue as a Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Very well, then. Did you challenge the Bureau's decision at that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I don't believe there were any further proceedings, Your Honour. May I just confer with counsel who was there at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm told that the decision was not rendered until after the trial had been concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: So far as the next ground is concerned, Your Honours, regarding the membership of the board of the Fund, I think the Court has clear the difference between the Prosecution and ourselves on that point. I needn't perhaps belabour it. Although I'm grateful to Mr. Yapa for reminding us of the mandate of the Fund, because when one looks at that, it's clear that it did involve exactly the same kinds of activities as Lord Hoffman was engaged in on behalf of Amnesty International. And as my learned friend Mr. Morrison showed, the true ground of decision was not that Lord Hoffman was a party in the sense that he was a litigant, but that he was associated very closely with the party because of identity of interest. I'm sure the Court has that point. And, Your Honour, if I need to respond to this, Mr. Yapa, if I understood him correctly, indicated that these two grounds of appeal were mutually inconsistent. Let me just point out that it is possible to advance alternative grounds of appeal. We do, of course, allege that the disqualification of Judge Odio-Benito on the ground of her membership of the Fund would have dated from the very beginning of the trial, but what we say, obviously, is that even if we are wrong about that, she became disqualified on other grounds with effect from the 8th of May, 1998, at the latest. And also, although I take Mr. Yapa's point that one should not cloister judges in ivory towers, I do submit that to some extent they must be cloistered in the courtroom. On Judge Karibi-Whyte, Your Honour, first of all, I don't agree with Mr. Yapa when he says that this was raised at the last moment. The evidence is quite clear that it was in fact raised, at the latest, in August of 1997. Mr. Yapa also says that it's a matter of conjecture as to whether the Judge was sleeping during those periods of time when the cameras were not trained on him. Your Honour, it's not a matter of conjecture; it's a matter of evidence, of inference. We have presented evidence, if the Court accepts it, that the Judge was sleeping on a very large number of days during the entire length of the trial, for very substantial periods of time. And if the question is: "What inference is to be drawn about the other periods of time," we have two alternatives. One would be to say that the Judge behaved in those unaccounted for periods in the same ways he did when the cameras were trained on him, and that's the inference that I would suggest would be logical. The other inference is that when the cameras were not on him, the Judge suddenly underwent some miraculous recovery or transformation that the cameras did not capture. Your Honour, I submit that that would be a much less logical conclusion. And the final thing is this: I kept waiting during Mr. Yapa's submissions to hear the Prosecution say that what went on in that courtroom was acceptable. I didn't hear that, and, Your Honour, I don't believe anyone in this courtroom would really believe it. And unless there are any questions, those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you want to add anything, Mr. Morrison?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Very little, Your Honour. I wasn't one of the illustrious counsel at trial, except at the very latter stages, and I must admit, the title is rather pleasing. The sleeping Judge point was, of course, taken on board by all of the defendants during the course of the motions, as my learned friend says, in August of 1997. The suggestion that it's been raised at the last moment by any one person is simply not supportable. I also waited in vain to hear something, but what I was waiting in vain to hear was some other construction of Rule 15(A) other than the obvious construction: "A Judge may not sit on a trial or appeal in any case which he" which must also mean she, "has a personal interest or concern in which he, or she, has, or has had, any association which might affect his impartiality." There is, in my submission, no intellectual way of reading or interpreting that intellectually honest way other than in the straightforward meaning of the words carefully chosen by the drafters. I'm grateful my learned friend didn't attempt to do so. No doubt he is an honest -- no doubt he is an honest man and of great professional integrity. The very lack of attempt to redefine that underscores the integrity and underscores what I said before about honour and duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. The last group, group 8, appeals against sentence. Mr. Staker.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: May it please the Chamber. Before I begin my submissions in relation to this ground of appeal, with the leave of the Bench, I just wondered if I might very briefly clarify one point relating to our submissions on superior responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We are a little limited. If you really have to put something, could you put it in writing so we can get on with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: With your leave, could I take 30 seconds?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's over. Thirty seconds are almost over. You'd better hurry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. It simply relates to a passing reference that Mr. Fenrick made to the Queen of the United Kingdom, and Mr. Morrison took the point up after a break yesterday to talk about her functions of conferring commissions on members of her armed forces. I just wanted to say that the reference to the Queen of the United Kingdom was intended by Mr. Fenrick merely to be a passing illustration. Our position is that de jure authority by itself is sufficient for superior responsibility even without de facto power, and I just wanted to make that clear, Your Honour. If it pleases the Chamber, I will try to avoid repeating anything in our briefs on the issue in relation to this ground of appeal, given that they are 88 pages long. Mr. Mucic, of course, also appeals against his own sentence on the grounds that it was excessive. We appeal on the ground that it was inadequate. So although there are two separate appeals, they are in that sense related. The first matter to mention is the standard of review in an appeal against sentence. We have made submissions on that in our brief, but I would draw attention to the fact that since our brief was filed, we now have some further authorities of this Tribunal on that. In particular, the decision of the Appeals Chamber in the Tadic sentencing appeal, at paragraph 20. I won't read that paragraph out. The issue then carries over into paragraph 21. There, what the Appeals Chamber applies is what I think we would call a discernible error test. They say that there must be a discernible error in the exercise of the Trial Chamber's discretion in sentencing, and there is a similar reference found in paragraph 73 of that judgement. This discernible error test was applied again by the Appeals Chamber in its judgement in the Aleksovski case of the 24th of March this year, at paragraph 187. We would submit that is now the test for the standard of review in an appeal against sentence. I would draw attention to paragraphs 5.27 and 5.28 of our reply brief, where we do make the point that in most national systems there is normally quite a developed body of jurisprudence on sentencing principles. The jurisprudence of this Tribunal at this early stage is still much more limited. It may therefore be that there is slightly greater scope than in some national systems for the Appeals Chamber to establish basic sentencing principles as a matter of first impression, more frequently than would happen in a national system, but we submit that it remains the case that the burden is always on the appellant to establish a discernible error. That applies to the Prosecution as much as to the Defence. We accept that the burden is on us in this appeal against Mr. Mucic's sentence, and we submit that we meet that burden. The errors that we submit are found in the sentencing part of the Trial Chamber's judgement in relation to Mr. Mucic are dealt with at length in our brief. The first error, we say, was the failure to give proper consideration to the gravity of the crimes in question. At paragraph 1225, the Trial Chamber said that the gravity of the crime was by far the most important consideration in sentencing. The Prosecution submits that this is a correct statement of basic sentencing principles and that this is now also further supported by subsequent decisions of this Tribunal. Again, in the Aleksovski appeal judgement, at paragraph 182, the Appeals Chamber quoted and endorsed the statement of the Trial Chamber in this case, to which I just referred, and the Appeals Chamber added that: "Consideration of the gravity of the conduct of the accused is normally the starting point for consideration of an appropriate sentence. The practice of the International Tribunal provides no exception." In the Aleksovski appeal, the Appeals Chamber in fact did increase the sentence on appeal, having found, and I quote: "………there was a discernible error in the Trial Chamber's exercise of discretion in imposing sentence. That error consisted of giving insufficient weight to the gravity of the conduct of the Appellant and failing to treat his position as commander as an aggravating feature in relation to his responsibility under Article 7(1) of the Statute. The sentence imposed by the Trial Chamber was manifestly inadequate." That was paragraph 187. And again in paragraph 182 of that judgement, the Appeals Chamber also quoted and endorsed a passage from the Kupreskic judgement, which stated that: "[t]he sentences to be imposed must reflect the inherent gravity of the criminal conduct of the accused. The determination of the gravity of the crime requires a consideration of the particular circumstances of the case, as well as the form and degree of participation of the accused in the crime." That quote comes from the Kupreskic judgement at paragraph 852. And for completeness, on the importance of gravity as a factor in sentencing, I would refer also to the Jelisic judgement at paragraph 121, and the Blaskic judgement at paragraph 765. The question then is whether the Trial Chamber in this case took the gravity of the crime as the starting point in sentence. We deal with this in our brief. We point out that the part of the Trial Chamber's judgement dealing with the sentencing of Mr. Mucic was five full pages long, and it was only in the very final paragraph, paragraph 1252, the last six lines on the last page, that the Trial Chamber added, basically as an afterthought, that it also considered the gravity of the offences. What the Trial Chamber took as its starting point in sentencing, and what occupied the bulk of those five pages, were matters such as the personal circumstances of the accused and the aggravating and mitigating circumstances. The Prosecution submits that to give primary consideration to these factors, and then only to consider the gravity of the crime as an afterthought, clearly involves a discernible error. The Prosecution's submissions on the principles of sentencing to be applied in a case of superior responsibility are set out in our brief, particularly, paragraphs 5.13 to paragraph 5.23. In support of that submission, we would now also refer to the Blaskic judgement at paragraph 789, in which the Trial Chamber said that: "When a commander fails in his duty to prevent the crime or punish the perpetrator thereof, he should receive a heavier sentence than the subordinates who committed the crime insofar as the failing conveys some tolerance, or even approval, on the part of the commander towards the commission of crimes by his subordinates, and thus contributes to encouraging the commission of new crimes. It would not, in fact, be consistent to punish a simple perpetrator with a sentence equal or greater to that of the commander." In relation to sentencing of the commander, reference can be made to the practice in the Aleksovski case. It would be our submission that one shouldn't seek to draw simple comparisons between a sentence imposed in one case and a sentence imposed in another, because every sentence will involve unique factors that aren't present in the other case. But it may be to some degree instructive to note that in Aleksovski the accused, who was convicted and sentenced, was also the commander of a prison. The scale and gravity of crimes committed against prisoners in the Celebici camp was, in our submission, evidently significantly greater than those in the Aleksovski case. On the other hand, in the present case, unlike Aleksovski, it wasn't suggested that the prison commander was actively involved in the commission of offences. Nevertheless, in the Aleksovski case, on appeal, the sentence was increased to seven years, with an indication given by the Appeals Chamber that the sentence would have been considerably longer but for certain special factors in that case, in particular, the factor that the accused had already been released after the Trial Chamber's judgement and was taken back into custody after some nine months at liberty. If one assumes that in the Aleksovski case the sentence normally would have been higher than seven years and compares that to the sentence in that case, as we say, we can't say that strict comparisons can be drawn, but that may be instructive to a degree. Our brief also deals with the aggravating and mitigating circumstances found by the Trial Chamber in this case, and presents submissions on why they would not justify such a significant reduction of sentence in this case. I won't repeat that. Before moving to the second error we say there is in the Trial Chamber's judgement, would this be a convenient moment to break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Certainly. We'll resume at 4.30, and we will be sitting through till 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Staker.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: May it please the Chamber. The second error which we submit is found in the Trial Chamber's judgement is dealt with in paragraphs 5.34 to 5.43 of our brief. The error which we submit exists was the failure of the Trial Chamber in sentencing to have regard to crimes committed in the camp other than those for which the accused had specifically been found guilty. The indictment in this case charged superior responsibility for certain specified crimes -- I withdraw that. The indictment in this case charged superior responsibility for various types of crimes committed in the camp. For instance, paragraph 22 charged Mr. Mucic with superior responsibility with respect to murders committed in the camp and then went on to say "including" and then it listed various murders. It's submitted that the use of the word "including" indicates that the allegation wasn't limited to the ones specified. We submit there's nothing impermissible in that form of pleading in the sense, Your Honour, that in some cases involving high-level perpetrators, crimes may be charged that involve thousands of victims, and we submit that it is sufficient to allege that thousands of victims were killed or suffered crimes committed against them. We submit it is not necessary to name every individual victim or to conclude that the person charged can only be convicted in relation to those victims that can be identified individually. In this case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Could I just ask you: Did the Prosecution seek findings in relation to the other murders at the time of the final addresses?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: My friend, I think, has answered that question. We submit, however, that the Trial Chamber made findings to that effect. It also specifically said that it did not regard the unspecified criminal acts as constituting any part of the charges against the accused, and it follows from that that they weren't taken into account in sentencing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The absence of any submission might have led them to that belief. I would not like to remain silent when you say that it was a permissible form of pleading. The illustration you gave would be sufficient, but not this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: We submit merely that in sentencing, one factor to be considered would be that in addition to the specific crimes found there were others. The third error in the Trial Chamber's judgement relates to Counts 36 and 37 relating to the inhumane conditions in the camp. The inhumane conditions that were found to exist were held to include deprivation of adequate water, food, medical care, sleeping and toilet facilities, and the general atmosphere of terror. These counts, therefore, didn't relate to specific acts or incidents in the camp but to the overall conditions, and we would submit that as the camp commander, Mr. Mucic must have borne more responsibility for this than his subordinates. And yet it will be seen that the same sentence was imposed on him as was imposed on his subordinates in respect of those counts. We submit the error, which is a discernible error, is the failure to consider his separate responsibility as commander of the camp. The fourth error we say relates to sentencing in relation to Count 48 relating to the unlawful confinement of civilians, in relation to this count, Mr. Mucic was found liable under Article 7(1) alone, as indicated in paragraph 5.48 of our brief. The Trial Chamber ignores this fact in its sentencing judgement, we submit, because it concludes at paragraph 1248 that "The criminal liability of Mr. Mucic has arisen entirely from his failure to exercise his superior authority for the beneficial purpose of the detainees in the Celebici prison camp". We also submit, for the reasons set out in our brief, that the Trial Chamber's judgement appeared to reflect a general attitude that the responsibility of Mr. Mucic was purely passive and vicarious, which, in our submission, fails to take adequate account of the fact that his liability under this count was one of a participant under Article 7(1). And also submitted in paragraph 5.51 of our brief, it's submitted that unlawful confinement is a serious offence in many national jurisdictions, and that in the context of international humanitarian law, the unlawful confinement of large numbers of people over a protracted period of time in inhumane conditions, in circumstances in which they're subject to being killed or tortured or otherwise mistreated is obviously a much more serious offence still, and the Prosecution submits that the failure of the Trial Chamber to take appropriate account of this involved a discernible error. The fifth error which we submit is found in the Trial Chamber's judgement relates to the fact that the Trial Chamber ordered that all of the sentences imposed were to be served concurrently. This argument's dealt with in paragraphs 5.54 to 5.75 of our brief. The Prosecution acknowledges that the Trial Chamber has a discretion to determine whether sentences are to be served consecutively or concurrently, but the Prosecution submits that a valid exercise of this discretion requires that the Trial Chamber give appropriate consideration to the question. The discretion should be exercised in a principled manner which reflects the aims and purposes of sentencing. We don't deny that examples can be found in judgements of Trial Chambers where sentences are ordered to be served concurrently without any reasoning or explanation being given. This practice has never been challenged on appeal before, but that does not mean that it necessarily constitutes a proper exercise of the Trial Chamber's discretion. In this case, the Trial Chamber gave only one reason for making all of the sentences concurrent. It said that in various paragraphs in the indictment, the accused had been charged accumulatively with more than one crime in respect of the same conduct. We submit that this cannot possibly provide any explanation for why sentences arising out of different conduct should necessarily be made consecutive. Our general proposition is that a person who commits multiple crimes as a result of multiple different criminal acts bears graver criminal responsibility than an accused who commits only one of those crimes and that it should be expected that this will be reflected in sentencing. To put it simply, all else being equal, a person who killed -- an accused who killed ten victims would be expected to receive a higher sentence than an accused who killed one victim. As we say in our brief, this doesn't mean that all sentences relating to different conduct should be made completely consecutive. If there are two separate crimes, each of which individually, had it been the sole crime, might have warranted a sentence of 20 years, the fact that there were two such similar crimes might lead to a sentence of 22 or 25 or some other period of imprisonment, but it would be greater than it would be if there were only one such criminal act to reflect the greater gravity of the accused's overall conduct. Furthermore, even where an accused is convicted of more than one crime in respect of the same conduct, a cumulative conviction of more than one crime for the same conduct, we submit that that doesn't necessarily mean that the sentences have to be completely concurrent. I made mention of this yesterday in relation to our submissions on cumulative convictions, that in certain national legal systems, the maximum sentence for a crime can be increased where that crime, at the same time, constituted another crime as well under the principles of ideal concurrence. In this case, the Trial Chamber imposed a sentence of seven years imprisonment in respect of all of the various crimes in respect of which Mr. Mucic had been found guilty. Thus he received the same sentence that he would have received if he'd committed only one of those various crimes. We submit that in this particular case, making all of the sentences completely concurrent failed to reflect the multiplicity of murders, tortures, rapes, mistreatment, inhuman conditions and unlawful confinements as a whole, and given the multiplicity of crimes, the Prosecution submits that there's a discernible error in the sentence. By way of remedy, the Prosecution submits that the Appeals Chamber can revise the Trial Chamber's sentence and substitute a new sentence. This is confirmed by the precedent [Realtime error read in error "president"] of the Aleksovski appeal judgement. And for the reasons given in the Prosecution appeal brief, the Prosecution now seeks a substituted sentence. If I cannot further assist, there are our submissions in relation to this ground of appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Morrison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just a mistake. You said -- was it confirmed by the president of the Aleksovski appeal? It's written here: "by the president."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Precedent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Precedent. All right. Then just check it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, may I tender the compliments and apologies for my learned friend Mr. Kuzmanovic, who can no longer be present. He, like my learned friend Mr. Ackerman, has had to return to the United States. As far as the matters are concerned, it is obvious, with great respect, what the Trial Chamber did in this case. They looked at the overall picture and they passed a global sentence, which they thought, in their judgement, having sat for 19 months listening, assessing witnesses, and assessing the defendant, often, as one would see in the judgement, to his detriment as to his personal behaviour, complaining, as they did -- that's contained in a separate ground, but it goes to the question of sentence -- complaining, as they did, that he didn't give evidence. I've raised objection to that in the brief. I don't repeat it, except to say it seems an extraordinary thing, bearing in mind the burden of proof. One suspects that having gone through that extended and difficult exercise, that they did take into account, as they were asked to take into account, the matters contained in the sentencing submissions and the matters which have been reput into the brief. I won't go through those in detail except to say this: It is extraordinary, and in my experience, and I suspect in the experience of most of Your Honours, that Prosecution witnesses -- and they were Prosecution witnesses -- should have said this about a defendant, Mr. Golubovic. This witness said in testimony, "If at least 20 per cent of the people in Bosnia had been like Mucic, there would have been no war." Well, bearing in mind the objectives of setting up this Tribunal, that was a pretty powerful comment to make. While giving testimony, he said of Mr. Mucic, "I don't think I'd be sitting here had it not been for him." In answer to the question, "Did people talk about Pavo Mucic in the village," he replied, "Of course they talked about him, all the people he helped. They were grateful and they talked about it." The witness Draganic included the observation that Pavo Mucic enjoyed a good reputation in the community as a fair and good man, and he acknowledged that Mr. Mucic had saved the life of both himself and his family, and he was grateful to him. Another prisoner from the camp. Grozdana Celez. This witness made reference to Mucic preventing the rape of a 13-year-old girl and gave testimony of the fact that he had paid money out of his own funds for her escape and was instrumental in saving other. Witness P testified that Mucic had made an urgent and forceful request for food for the prisoners in Celebici, and further, giving what he described as his personal subjective opinion, answered yes to this question: "Can it be said that Mr. Mucic was protecting the prisoners to a certain extent as far as he was able?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There's a complaint about the speed, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm reading again. Witness T, during cross-examination by my learned friend Mr. Ackerman, the following verbatim exchange: "I think you told us yesterday, and I just want to make certain that I understood you correctly, that these releases of prisoners were primarily due to the efforts of Mr. Mucic, Mr. Pavo Mucic, who was constantly agitating for the young -- for the old or young or the innocent to be released from Celebici. Is that correct or not?" Answer: "Yes." Question: "Mr. Mucic helped the Serbs as much as he could, did he not?" Answer: "Yes." Now, if those don't go to most of the issues complained of by the Prosecution in this case, it's very difficult to see what does. What the Defence has complained about in its appeal and submits in its appeal is that those factors weren't taken sufficiently into account, and at the time that observation was put into a submission, the judgement in Aleksovski wasn't available. It is now a completely different case, and of course Mr. Aleksovski was originally sentenced to two and a half years. That was increased to seven years, an identical sentence to that passed on this defendant. It is said in respect of Mr. Aleksovski that one of the reasons it wasn't longer was because he's been at liberty. That's maybe slightly odd, because this defendant has been imprisoned for four years and three months awaiting today. It seems rather to Mr. Aleksovski's benefit that he was at liberty. I'm sure he was happier with that than had been in prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I didn't stop Mr. Staker when he said that, but what was said in Aleksovski was the issue of what is called perhaps a misleadingly double jeopardy in a Crown appeal. That's why it was lower than it would otherwise have been, and plus the fact that he had been allowed out, or at liberty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honour, with respect, double jeopardy does apply, of course, in this case, as from my own experience it would apply in an Attorney General's reference in the United Kingdom. Where somebody has had a sentence and he's been looking forward for a number of years to a potential release date, that is, of course, always, and quite properly, taken into account. I do revisit the case of Von Leeb -- it's in the brief, and I don't repeat that -- as to give an example of how someone who is even a supreme commander, and who is effectively convicted in respect of acts of murder committed by subordinates, receives a sentence, as he did, of three years before the Nuremberg Tribunal, a tribunal whose sentence options included, of course, the death penalty. If I was to go beyond that which I've gone, I would simply be trespassing on the 56 pages, I think, that were written in response to the Prosecution. It's a tempting trespass, but when I look into Judge Hunt's eyes, the temptation vanishes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Morrison. Mr. Moran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, so I won't be tempted to read from the brief, I brought one sheet of legal-sized paper. May it please the Court. I have both an issue on appeal and then a suggestion -- and I'll do the issue on appeal first, of course -- on whether the assessment of punishment in this case resulted in an ex post facto increase in the maximum punishment. And the basic argument, without going over in great detail what I've briefed, is this: The Geneva Conventions are not some kind of new international penal code. It was never meant to be that. In fact, there seems to be a presumption at the time the -- Judge Riad is looking like -- questioning that. Your Honour, one of the things I cited was the -- I cited in my brief, is the report from the US Foreign Relations Committee on ratification by the United States of the Conventions in 1956, and the phrase "not an international penal code" comes from that report. It appears that what was expected would be that the Conventions would be enforced through national courts. This Tribunal is the first international court since what, 1948? And so that would seem to be what the authors of the Convention presumed. They also provided universal jurisdiction, but that universal jurisdiction simply allows any state to assume jurisdiction over war crimes; does not require them to do so. And another example from my brief is the United States War Crimes Act, which limits the jurisdiction of United States courts to cases involving United States citizens, nationals, or members of the United States military as either a perpetrator or a victim. There's no evidence before this Court that there's any state other than those in the former Yugoslavia that had any jurisdiction to try these offences prior to the creation of this Tribunal in May of 1993, which was after the acts complained of in the indictment. I believe it was May the 20-something, if I've got it right. I keep getting a mental block on that date, but in any case ... Therefore the only punishment ranges which were available to a court which we know had jurisdiction to try these allegations were those in the SFRY Penal Code. We presented an expert, Professor Tomic, from the law faculty of the University of Sarajevo, and in his report, what Dr. Tomic said was that the maximum term of incarceration which could be assessed by a Yugoslavian court under the then Penal Code was 15 years, with one exception: It was a case in which the death penalty was allowed. The Court could assess the death penalty, and then immediately, as a grant of commutation, reduce that death penalty to 20 years. It's my position that that means that the maximum punishment that this Court can assess for an offence prior to the date of creation of the Tribunal, prior to that May 1993 date, is 15 years, and the reason behind that is this Court lacks the jurisdiction to assess the death penalty. So it cannot assess the death penalty and then, as a matter of grace, reduce it to 20 years immediately. I think this issue's been pretty well briefed, and if there's no questions on that, a suggestion to the Court: We have, of course, raised issues of sufficiency of the evidence on some counts. It is quite conceivable that we would be successful on some of those and unsuccessful on others, and if that were to be the case, and I'll use the examples of the first four counts, if the Court were to find the evidence insufficient and enter an acquittal on Counts 1 and 2 but not 3 and 4, the sentences are both identical, which are 20 years, I would submit, as Mr. Staker just said, an accused who kills ten persons should receive a higher sentence than a person who kills only one person, if the Court finds insufficient evidence on either Counts 1 and 2 or 3 and 4, then the Court should reassess the punishment on the remaining count. With that, Your Honours, I thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moran. Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Sorry. May it please the Court. Mr. Landzo was convicted of killing three persons, of torturing four persons, and of causing great suffering or serious injury to body or health and cruel treatment of three persons. Draza Erdemovic entered a guilty plea to one count of crimes against humanity for his participation in the execution of approximately 1.200 unarmed civilian Muslims. That was the original allegation that he pled guilty to. In the end result, after the appeals, he confessed and was found guilty of killing at least 75 persons in one day, the 16th of July, 1995. He received a sentence of five years, and today he's walking around The Hague. There's some injustice there. Mr. Landzo was sentenced to 15 years. I know there's a lot of other factors to take into consideration in the Erdemovic sentencing, but not so different from Mr. Landzo. He offered to cooperate with the Prosecution. Putting the Erdemovic decision aside, in the newly decided Tadic sentencing appeal, the Appeals Chamber held that the sentences must reflect the relative significance of the role of the appellant in the broader context of the conflict in the former Yugoslavia. This Chamber must consider the Tadic factor, Landzo's place in the overall scheme in the war in the former Yugoslavia. In the Tadic sentence appeal, the Trial Chamber -- I mean the Appeals Chamber held that persons who set policy --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel be reminded to slow down when reading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Sinatra, it's a fault that everybody has, I'm afraid. If you read, you do speed up, and they're having trouble with the translations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: My apologies to the Interpretation Department. In the Tadic decision, it says that: "The persons who set out policy and order large-scale atrocities should be punished more harshly than defendants who, while guilty of personally committing offences, are minor players in a much larger game controlled by others." There is no one who was more a minor player in the conflict in Yugoslavia than Esad Landzo was. I think the Trial Chamber failed to consider Mr. Landzo's overall situation. It failed to consider the total lack of authority of this young boy sucked up in the invasion of his home. Landzo had no authority for the conduct of war. He had no responsibility for policy decisions. He had no military training or authority. In short, his role was very insignificant in the broader context of the conflict in the former Yugoslavia. Now, Mr. Staker had talked about earlier diminished mental responsibility that was taken into consideration by the Trial Chamber. The only reference that the Trial Chamber made that it considered Mr. Landzo's mental state was in paragraph 1283 of the judgement, and going down to the second line, it says: "While the special defence of diminished responsibility raised by the Defence has been rejected by the Trial Chamber, the Trial Chamber may nonetheless take note of the evidence presented by the numerous mental-health experts, which collectively reveals a picture of Mr. Landzo's personality traits that contributes to our consideration of appropriate sentence." What we submit to the Appeals Chamber right now is that clearly the Trial Chamber did not and could not quantify any amount of sentence that it applied to the sentence for Mr. Landzo that applied to diminished mental responsibility. It didn't recognise that Mr. Landzo's responsibility was diminished with respect to the sentence. Merely stating that they took into account his mental traits does not recognise diminished mental responsibility even in application to mitigation of punishment. What we're asking the Appeals Chamber to do now is if it -- this is in the alternative, as Mr. Murphy, Professor Murphy, had discussed earlier -- if you find that the defence of diminished mental responsibility did not rise to the threshold level to be a complete defence under Rule 67, then please find that there was sufficient proof in the evidence presented in the case-in-chief to warrant diminished mental responsibility, recognised and stated in the judgement, with a quantified amount of time that he was given credit for. So if he didn't meet the threshold in the case-in-chief for complete defence of diminished mental responsibility, then the defence should be recognised in the sentencing now and used in the alternative to lower his sentence. Merely stating that they took into consideration the evidence by the mental-health experts of his mental traits does not rise to the level of diminished mental responsibility. But the proof was sufficient, when this Court finally does offer a definition, that in mitigation of punishment, we did prove diminished mental responsibility. And for mitigation of punishment, the Trial Court clearly did not say, "Well, we sentenced him to 15 years, but because of his state of diminished mental responsibility, we reduce that sentence to 5 years or 10 years." That's not clear. It's nowhere stated or recognised by the Trial Chamber. Another thing: Mr. Staker said earlier that Mr. Landzo's sentence was proportionally reduced in comparison to the sentence of Hazim Delic. So he's claiming that there was a proportionate reduction based upon diminished mental responsibility, but that's not true. Hazim Delic was charged with different counts under the indictment. Mr. Landzo was never charged with rape, and he was not considered to have any -- well, he was not charged with the same counts in the indictment and not charged with the same crimes as Mr. Delic was. Mr. Landzo requests this Trial Chamber now just to reconsider the evidence that we submitted in sentencing, reconsider the fragile mental condition of Mr. Landzo before the outbreak of the aggression, his lack of ability to exercise his own free will, and also, in light of Tadic, to revisit all of the evidence presented. In America it's called due process of law, in the United Kingdom it's called law of the land, and other nations have variations on the Latin phrase, but at their core, they're shorthand for the notion of sovereign decency, for the basic profound idea that there is an inviolate dignity in every man. It's not a theoretical concept but clearly bought in the long and bloody experiences in human history. In Tokyo, the Tribunal's majority judgement was followed by four separate or dissenting opinions and one concurring opinion. Three dissenters: Justice Bernard of France, Justice Pahl [phoen] of India, and Justice Roelling [phoen] of the Netherlands. In his dissenting judgement, Justice Bernard concluded that a verdict reached by a Tribunal after a defective procedure cannot be a valid one. I just ask that you listen to all the arguments here today and take heed and preserve our legacy of justice that we've created so far. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sinatra. Now, Mr. Staker, you have a reply to Mr. Morrison, plus a response to Mr. Morrison, and a response to each of the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have just a few very brief points, beginning with Mr. Morrison's response. He said merely that it's clear from the sentencing judgement that the Trial Chamber's sentence was based on an overall picture of all the facts. We don't suggest otherwise. The basis of our appeal against sentence in the case of Mr. Mucic is not that the overall picture of the facts wasn't looked at, but rather that incorrect principles of sentencing were applied, and that inappropriate weight and consideration was given to the way that the facts were assessed in relation to what the appropriate sentence would be, and that significance wasn't given to certain factors which we submit, in fact, were very important. Then to Mr. Moran on behalf of Mr. Delic. He made the argument that it would constitute an ex post facto law for a sentence any higher than 15 years to be imposed because of the state of the law in the former Yugoslavia at the time. I think a short answer to that submission is provided by the decision of the Appeals Chamber in the Tadic sentencing appeal, paragraph 21. And in accordance with the principles of precedent enunciated in the Aleksovski appeal judgement, we submit that there have been no cogent reasons advanced why that should now be reconsidered. But further support for the proposition that the Tribunal is not bound by maximum sentences under the law in the former Yugoslavia is now to be found in decisions of Trial Chambers in the Kupreskic judgement, paragraph 846, and the proposition is also supported in practice by the Blaskic judgement, where a sentence of 45 years was imposed. I note that both judgements are presently subject to pending appeals, but I cite them merely as recent precedents. Mr. Moran also made the point that if any of the convictions are overturned in relation to Mr. Delic, then in accordance with the principle that I outlined, the sentence ought to be reduced somewhat to take account of the fact that the overall responsibility of Mr. Delic would then be somewhat less. That might perhaps be a consequence to be drawn from the principle of sentencing, which I have submitted is the correct one, but I would also submit that in this particular case, that wasn't the basis of the Trial Chamber's decision. The Trial Chamber ordered that all of the sentences were to be completely concurrent, and the Trial Chamber clearly considered that the sentence imposed on every one of those crimes, or every one of the counts, would have been the appropriate sentence even if that count had been the sole count for which the accused had been found guilty in that case. I turn then to the submissions made by Ms. Sinatra on behalf of Mr. Landzo. First, reference was made to the Erdemovic case. I think that comparison has already been dealt with in our briefs. Very shortly, we submit that the factor of duress that existed in the Erdemovic case made it truly exceptional, and it's very hard to draw any comparison from that in this case. I think it was -- in the Appeals Chamber a comment was made that here was someone basically in the position of having to either kill or be killed himself, and we submit there's absolutely no comparison here in this case. There is no suggestion whatever that Mr. Landzo was somehow forced or would have faced adverse consequences had he not committed these crimes. Mention was then made of his offer to cooperate with the Prosecutor. We submit that, first of all, that's a mischaracterisation of what occurred, and we would also say that it is, in fact, dealt with by the Trial Chamber in its sentencing reasoning, unless I have misunderstood the submission being made. In paragraph 1279 there is a reference to discussions that were entered into with a view to the possibility of a plea agreement, and the Trial Chamber held that that was not an offer of cooperation that would justify a reduction in sentence. Paragraph 1282 is also relevant in that regard. The next point made related to the observation in the Tadic appeal that sentencing should reflect the relative significance of the perpetrator in the overall events in the former Yugoslavia. Our submission is that this is, in fact, something that the Trial Chamber did have regard to, if one looks at paragraph 1280 of the Trial Chamber's judgement. The next point was that the Trial Chamber did not or could not quantify the degree of diminished mental responsibility. If I understand this submission, basically it's an adoption of the submissions that were already made in relation to the ground of appeal dealing with diminished mental responsibility, and I think the response we made in relation to that ground of appeal sufficiently covers this point. It was said by Ms. Sinatra that it can't be said that based on diminished mental responsibility a lower sentence was imposed on Mr. Landzo than was on his co-accused Mr. Delic. I didn't intend to say that that was the case. I think I did say that it was impossible to know to what extent that factor might have resulted in a reduction of sentence, but that when one compared, in particular, the sentences imposed where they were both found guilty in relation to the same counts, the difference does seem to suggest that different factors were taken into account in relation to Mr. Landzo. The final submission made by Ms. Sinatra was a request to the Appeals Chamber that it reconsider all the evidence relative to sentencing in this case. My reply to that is simply that this is basically a request for a de novo sentencing by the Appeals Chamber. We have already dealt with the standard of review on appeal, and we submit that that would not be something that the Appeals Chamber should appropriately do, if the Chamber pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is it correct for international criminal trials, that where sentences are concurrent, that the longer of those sentences, if there be a longer one, is intended to represent the appropriate sentence for all of the charges which have been established?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: That -- if I could clarify the question. Is the question whether it would be appropriate to establish such a practice or whether such a practice has been established?.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, No. I want to know -- this is matter raised by Mr. Moran, which you haven't dealt with in your response. Certainly in the jurisdiction with which I am familiar, for a very long time, until fairly recently, it was the accepted law that you could have concurrent or consecutive or cumulative sentencing provided that the total was the fair and appropriate figure for the totality of the criminality involved, and if you made them concurrent, then the longer of the sentences if there be a longer one, or if they're all the same the total length, was intended to represent an appropriate sentence for all of the charges which were found proven. Now, is that appropriate and has it been the practice for the international criminal law applied by this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would submit that there's no basis for suggesting that that has been the practice. I would submit that there -- I can think of no reason why it would be inappropriate for that to become the practice. In this case, I submit that was not the practice. The Trial Chamber simply imposed sentences and said completely concurrent without addressing its mind to the question. The practice in this Tribunal has, in fact, been somewhat varied. Particularly in the Rwanda Tribunal, but also in this Tribunal in the Blaskic judgement, the approach adopted was that one single global sentence was imposed in respect of all of the counts on which the accused was found guilty. And that is, as I understand it, the practice in France, and I would assume various other countries, particularly those with similar legal systems. The difficulty that that approach poses in the context of this Tribunal is where, on appeal, acquittals on a few of multiple counts are overturned, it's then not clear what the remaining sentence should be. Now, it may be that if the Appeals Chamber can revise a sentence on appeal it can deal with it in that way, but by imposing separate sentences, it makes it clearer what the position is if some are overturned. On the other hand, if separate sentences are imposed and they're all ordered to become concurrent, then -- if you understand what I am mean. If we said, if this were the only crime, this would be the sentence we impose, make them all concurrent, and then if any of the counts are overturned on appeal it's easy to see what's left. The problem is when you do that, the overall global sentence may not take account of the fact that there were various crimes. The overall sentence would simply be the highest of one individual sentence. I think the solution that Your Honour has suggested may be a very practical way of addressing this in the practice of the Tribunal. But as I say, there has been, so far as I'm aware, no pronouncement of the principle that should be adopted in dealing with this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You see, you said earlier that it was a discretionary matter, whether they should be concurrent or cumulative. That must surely -- the exercise of that discretion must surely depend upon whether or not the total sentence which is finally imposed is appropriate for the total criminality involved. So that if you have two 20-year sentences, if you made them cumulative it would be 40 years. If you make them concurrent, it's 20 years. That's rather a large difference, and it seems to me that that's a matter which would have to be taken into account in determining whether they should be concurrent or cumulative. And that works both ways. The totality of criminality has to be fair to both the Prosecution which prosecutes on behalf of the International Community and the accused who has to serve the sentence. So that that must be a matter to be taken into account in the exercise of that discretion. Now, what you have to say then is that the total figure here should it have been 40 years or it should have been 20 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: That's the -- I know the Rules say that the sentences shall be either consecutive or concurrent. My submission is they don't have to be necessarily completely consecutive or completely concurrent. It may be that a Trial Chamber would feel, if there are three murders, that each of the murders, had it been the only murder, would have merited 20 years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That would depend on whether they're separate counts, which is another pleading problem with the Prosecution's style of pleading. Sometimes you have a large number of killings within the one count. There it would be appropriate just to have the one sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: I would not submit that it should make a difference to sentencing whether three murders are charged in one count or the three murders are charged in three separate counts, but my submission is simply if there are three murders, each of which had it been the only murder, would merit a 20-year sentence. We don't suggest that they should necessarily be completely consecutive so that there's a 60-year sentence. On the other hand, make them all completely concurrent would lead to a global 20-year sentence, which is the same as would be imposed if there had only been one murder. That might not adequately reflect the total criminality involved and it may be more appropriate to impose a sentence of, as I said, in the Trial Chamber's discretion, 22, 24, whatever the Trial Chamber considered appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: By making them partly concurrent and partly cumulative.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: That would be one way of doing it. The other would be to impose a single sentence to indicate the single sentence reflects the totality. The other would be to impose completely concurrent sentences, but possibly to make them higher to reflect the fact and to say -- I mean, there are different combinations and permutations. Our submission is simply that the Trial Chamber must, in the exercise of its discretion, address its mind to the totality of the criminal conduct, not to look at each count in isolation, impose a sentence, and then, without addressing its mind to the question at all, simply say: Serve concurrent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, what you are really saying, if I interpret you correctly, is that whether they should be concurrent, or cumulative, or partly one and partly the other, you must take into account the totality of the criminality in determining how you exercise that discretion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: That is our submission, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there anything further you want to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Morrison, you have the right of reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: It comes to this: On behalf of the bar, may I thank the translators and the transcribers for their hard work in this case. I think all the points have been heard. I think they will be grateful that they don't have to assist us in airing them anymore. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Moran, do you want to reply to anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just very briefly. I think, if I understood Mr. Staker just a minute ago, he was saying that essentially the total sentence ought to reflect the total criminality, and I would agree with him on that. And if the Appeals Chamber finds that there is less total criminality, I think we all agree. And with that, I will join Mr. Morrison. There's been many interpreters here. I'm seeing some old friends sitting up in the windows that have had to put up with me and my Texanisms for roughly three years now in translating the different languages, and I am very grateful to them and the rest of the staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have nothing more on the issue of sentencing, but I too would like to thank not only the interpreters, but these court reporters and the registry and the security guards, who have been most helpful with us throughout this long, challenging period of time we've been here, and I thank you for listening to us today. I think my colleague has something more to say, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the heat of battle earlier on, I found myself later unsure of the position about the proof of the Constitution of Costa Rica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, that's a point that I've got noted here to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What we need to know is whether the Prosecution accepts as accurate the translation of the whole of the Constitution of Costa Rica in the version which has been used by both sides, that published by Oceania Publications in a book called "Constitutions of the Countries of the World," edited by a Mr. Flanz, which was issued in May 1995. Now, Mr. Staker, have you got any idea when we might get some response from you about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would hope to be in a position to find out fairly quickly. How long it would take? I don't know what the answer to that question would be, but I would hope that we could presumably file our response to that in a very short time frame. We could do that in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: In the document itself, it shows when various amendments were made. There were none made between 1992 and 1995, so far as I can see. What you'd have to check is to whether there were any made subsequently which relate to any of the issues that have been raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hope the Chamber appreciates that I'm not trying to be difficult or overly technical. I mean, publications can contain omissions or errors, and when so much hinges on this, we feel it is necessary not to simply accept the publication as necessarily authoritative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I understand your point. My concern before was simply that I hoped that it didn't depend upon who was paying for it, seeing it all comes out of the same pocket eventually.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: That was not the consideration, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, the Appeals Chamber is very grateful to all of the counsel who have assisted us, and we will reserve our decision. On behalf of the Appeals Chamber, I too would like to thank the translators and the court reporters, who have been given a very thorough workout in this appeal, operating, as they do, outside the usual situation of a trial, where there are sometimes pauses between questions and answers. With that comment, we will adjourn.
